<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a non-empty set. A \emph{finitely additive probability measure} on $X$ is a map
$$
\mu:\mathcal P(X)\longrightarrow [0,1]
$$
such that the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mu(X)=1$;
    \item if $A,B\subseteq X$ and $A\cap B=\varnothing$, then
    $$
    \mu(A\sqcup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B).
    $$
\end{enumerate}
We denote by $\operatorname{PM}(X)$ the set of all finitely additive probability measures on $X$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a group. A measure $\mu\in\operatorname{PM}(G)$ is called \emph{left $G$-invariant} if
$$
\mu(gA)=\mu(A) \text{ for every }g\in G\text{ and every }A\subseteq G.
$$
Similarly, $\mu$ is called \emph{right $G$-invariant} if
$$
\mu(Ag)=\mu(A) \text{ for every }g\in G\text{ and every }A\subseteq G.
$$
If both conditions hold, then $\mu$ is called \emph{bi-invariant}.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A discrete group $G$ is called \emph{amenable} if there exists a left $G$-invariant finitely additive probability measure on $G$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Every finite group is amenable. Indeed, if $G$ is finite, then
$$
\mu(A)=\frac{|A|}{|G|} \text{ for every }A\subseteq G
$$
defines an element of $\operatorname{PM}(G)$. Since left multiplication by any $g\in G$ is a bijection, one has $|gA|=|A|$, and therefore $\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
A \emph{mean} on $X$ is a linear functional
$$
m:\ell^\infty(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb R
$$
such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $m(\mathbf 1_X)=1$;
    \item if $f\in\ell^\infty(X)$ and $f\geq 0$, then $m(f)\geq 0$.
\end{enumerate}
We denote by $\mathcal M(X)$ the set of all means on $X$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A mean $m\in\mathcal M(G)$ is called \emph{left $G$-invariant} if
$$
m(g\cdot f)=m(f) \text{ for every }g\in G\text{ and every }f\in\ell^\infty(G).
$$
Right invariant and bi-invariant means are defined analogously.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
There is an affine bijection
$$
\mathcal M(X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{PM}(X), \ m\longmapsto\mu_m,
$$
where
$$
\mu_m(A)=m(\mathbf 1_A) \text{ for every }A\subseteq X.
$$
Under this bijection, left $G$-invariant means on $G$ correspond exactly to left $G$-invariant finitely additive probability measures on $G$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
For a discrete group $G$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $G$ is amenable;
    \item there exists a left $G$-invariant mean on $\ell^\infty(G)$;
    \item there exists a right $G$-invariant mean on $\ell^\infty(G)$;
    \item there exists a bi-invariant mean on $\ell^\infty(G)$;
    \item there exists a left $G$-invariant finitely additive probability measure on $G$;
    \item there exists a bi-invariant finitely additive probability measure on $G$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
A countable discrete group $G$ satisfies the \emph{left F{\o}lner condition} if, for every finite subset $K\subseteq G$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a non-empty finite subset $F\subseteq G$ such that
$$
\frac{|F\setminus kF|}{|F|}<\varepsilon \text{ for every }k\in K.
$$
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
For a countable discrete group $G$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $G$ is amenable;
    \item $G$ satisfies the left F{\o}lner condition;
    \item $G$ satisfies the right F{\o}lner condition;
    \item $G$ admits a left F{\o}lner sequence;
    \item $G$ admits a right F{\o}lner sequence.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
The group $\mathbb Z^d$ is amenable. Indeed, the sequence
$$
F_n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}^d, \ n\geq 1,
$$
is a F{\o}lner sequence. Consequently, every finitely generated abelian group is amenable, and permanence under directed unions implies that every abelian group is amenable.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
A group $G$ is said to be \emph{paradoxical} if there exist pairwise disjoint subsets
$$
A_1,\dots,A_n,B_1,\dots,B_m\subseteq G
$$
and elements
$$
g_1,\dots,g_n,h_1,\dots,h_m\in G
$$
such that
$$
G=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^n g_iA_i=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^m h_jB_j.
$$
In this case, we say that $G$ admits a \emph{paradoxical decomposition}.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
The free group $F_2=\langle a,b\rangle$ is not amenable. Indeed, by decomposing reduced words according to their first letter, one obtains a paradoxical decomposition of $F_2$. This is the classical obstruction behind the non-amenability of free groups of rank at least two.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
For a countable discrete group $G$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $G$ is amenable;
    \item $G$ satisfies the F{\o}lner condition;
    \item $G$ does not admit a paradoxical decomposition.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a discrete group. The following assertions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item if $G$ is amenable and $H\leq G$, then $H$ is amenable;
    \item if $G$ is amenable and $N\trianglelefteq G$, then $G/N$ is amenable;
    \item if $N\trianglelefteq G$ and both $N$ and $G/N$ are amenable, then $G$ is amenable;
    \item finite direct products of amenable groups are amenable;
    \item directed unions of amenable groups are amenable;
    \item if $G$ is countable, then $G$ is amenable if and only if every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is amenable.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
Finite groups, abelian groups, locally finite groups and solvable groups are amenable.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Finite groups are amenable by the normalized counting measure. Every finitely generated abelian group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^d\times F$ for some $d\geq 0$ and some finite abelian group $F$, and is therefore amenable. Permanence under directed unions then shows that every abelian group is amenable. Every finitely generated subgroup of a locally finite group is finite, so local finiteness implies amenability. Finally, solvable groups are obtained from abelian groups by finitely many extensions, and amenability is preserved under extensions.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a group and let $X$ be a non-empty set. A \emph{left action} of $G$ on $X$ is a map
$$
G\times X\longrightarrow X, \ (g,x)\longmapsto gx,
$$
such that
$$
e_Gx=x \text{ and } g(hx)=(gh)x
$$
for every $g,h\in G$ and every $x\in X$. If $X$ is a topological space and every map $x\longmapsto gx$ is a homeomorphism, then the action is called a \emph{topological action}. Since $G$ is discrete, this is equivalent to continuity of the action map $G\times X\longrightarrow X$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a topological space. The \emph{Borel $\sigma$-algebra} of $X$, denoted by $\mathcal B(X)$, is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra of subsets of $X$ containing every open subset of $X$. The elements of $\mathcal B(X)$ are called the \emph{Borel subsets} of $X$.

A \emph{Borel probability measure} on $X$ is a map
$$
\nu:\mathcal B(X)\longrightarrow [0,1]
$$
such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\nu(X)=1$;
    \item for every sequence $(A_n)_{n\geq 1}$ of pairwise disjoint Borel subsets of $X$, one has
    $$
    \nu\left(\bigsqcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\nu(A_n).
    $$
\end{enumerate}
We denote by $\operatorname{Prob}(X)$ the set of all Borel probability measures on $X$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Let $G\curvearrowright X$ be a topological action on a compact Hausdorff space. A Borel probability measure $\nu\in\operatorname{Prob}(X)$ is called \emph{$G$-invariant} if
$$
\nu(gA)=\nu(A)
$$
for every $g\in G$ and every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
For a countable discrete group $G$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $G$ is amenable;
    \item every continuous action of $G$ on a non-empty compact Hausdorff space admits a $G$-invariant Borel probability measure;
    \item every continuous action of $G$ on a non-empty compact metrizable space admits a $G$-invariant Borel probability measure.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
A \emph{groupoid} is a small category in which every arrow is invertible. We identify each object with its identity arrow and denote the set of all units by $\mathcal G^{(0)}$. Equivalently,
$$
\mathcal G^{(0)} = \{\gamma^{-1}\gamma\mid\gamma\in\mathcal G\} = \{\gamma\gamma^{-1}\mid\gamma\in\mathcal G\}.
$$
For $\gamma\in\mathcal G$, its source and range are
$$
s(\gamma)=\gamma^{-1}\gamma, \ r(\gamma)=\gamma\gamma^{-1},
$$
respectively. The set of composable pairs is
$$
\mathcal G^{(2)} = \{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal G\times\mathcal G\mid s(\alpha)=r(\beta)\}.
$$
For subsets $U,V\subseteq\mathcal G$, we define
$$
UV = \{\alpha\beta\mid\alpha\in U,\ \beta\in V,\ s(\alpha)=r(\beta)\}
$$
and
$$
U^{-1}=\{\gamma^{-1}\mid\gamma\in U\}.
$$
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
A \emph{topological groupoid} is a groupoid $\mathcal G$ endowed with a topology such that the source and range maps
$$
s,r:\mathcal G\longrightarrow\mathcal G^{(0)},
$$
the inversion map
$$
\mathcal G\longrightarrow\mathcal G, \ \gamma\longmapsto\gamma^{-1},
$$
and the multiplication map
$$
\mathcal G^{(2)}\longrightarrow\mathcal G, \ (\alpha,\beta)\longmapsto\alpha\beta,
$$
are continuous, where $\mathcal G^{(2)}$ carries the subspace topology inherited from $\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$. The unit space $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is always equipped with the subspace topology.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
A topological groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called \emph{\'{e}tale} if the source map
$$
s:\mathcal G\longrightarrow\mathcal G^{(0)}
$$
is a local homeomorphism. Equivalently, the range map
$$
r:\mathcal G\longrightarrow\mathcal G^{(0)}
$$
is a local homeomorphism.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal G$ be a topological groupoid. A subset $U\subseteq\mathcal G$ is called a \emph{bisection} if the restrictions
$$
r|_U:U\longrightarrow r(U), \ s|_U:U\longrightarrow s(U),
$$
are injective. If $U$ is open, then it is called an \emph{open bisection}. When $\mathcal G$ is \'{e}tale and $U$ is an open bisection, both restrictions are homeomorphisms onto open subsets of $\mathcal G^{(0)}$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal G$ be an \'{e}tale groupoid. Then $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is open in $\mathcal G$, the maps $r$ and $s$ are open, and the open bisections form a basis for the topology of $\mathcal G$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
An \'{e}tale groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called \emph{ample} if its compact open bisections form a basis for its topology.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal G$ be a Hausdorff ample groupoid. Under setwise multiplication and inversion, $\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ is an inverse semigroup. Its idempotents are precisely the compact open subsets of the unit space:
$$
E\bigl(\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)\bigr) = \{C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}\mid C\text{ is compact and open}\}.
$$
For compact open subsets $C,D\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$, one has $CD=C\cap D$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
If $\mathcal G$ is a Hausdorff ample groupoid, then $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space with a basis of compact open subsets. In particular, $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is a locally compact Boolean space. Throughout the remainder of the paper, all ample groupoids are assumed to be Hausdorff unless explicitly stated otherwise.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
Let $Y\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$. The set $Y$ is called \emph{invariant} if
$$
s(\gamma)\in Y \ \Longleftrightarrow \ r(\gamma)\in Y
$$
for every $\gamma\in\mathcal G$. The \emph{reduction} of $\mathcal G$ to $Y$ is the subgroupoid
$$
\mathcal G|_Y = r^{-1}(Y)\cap s^{-1}(Y) = \{\gamma\in\mathcal G\mid r(\gamma)\in Y,\ s(\gamma)\in Y\}.
$$
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{groupoid-orbit-isotropy}
Let $u\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$. The \emph{isotropy group at $u$} is
$$
\mathcal G_u^u=\{\gamma\in\mathcal G\mid s(\gamma)=u=r(\gamma)\},
$$
and the \emph{orbit of $u$} is
$$
\mathcal O_u=r\bigl(s^{-1}(u)\bigr)=\{r(\gamma)\mid\gamma\in\mathcal G,\ s(\gamma)=u\}.
$$
The groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called \emph{transitive} if it has a single orbit, equivalently, if for every $u,v\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$ there exists $\gamma\in\mathcal G$ such that
$$
s(\gamma)=v, \ r(\gamma)=u.
$$
It is called \emph{principal} if every isotropy group is trivial, that is,
$$
\mathcal G_u^u=\{u\}
$$
for every $u\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
A topological groupoid is called \emph{discrete} if its arrow space is endowed with the discrete topology. It is called \emph{countable} if its arrow space is countable. Thus a countable discrete groupoid is a groupoid with countably many arrows equipped with the discrete topology.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
Let $Z$ be a topological space. A function $f:Z\longrightarrow R$ is called \emph{locally constant} if every $z\in Z$ has an open neighbourhood on which $f$ is constant. Its support is
$$
\operatorname{supp}(f) = \overline{\{z\in Z\mid f(z)\neq 0\}}.
$$
If $f$ is locally constant, then $\{z\in Z\mid f(z)\neq 0\}$ is clopen and therefore coincides with $\operatorname{supp}(f)$.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal G$ be a Hausdorff ample groupoid. The \emph{Steinberg algebra} of $\mathcal G$ over $R$, denoted by $A_R(\mathcal G)$, is the $R$-module of all locally constant, compactly supported functions
$$
f:\mathcal G\longrightarrow R,
$$
with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication and with convolution product
$$
(f\ast g)(\gamma)=\sum_{\alpha\beta=\gamma}f(\alpha)g(\beta), \ \gamma\in\mathcal G.
$$
The sum is finite because $\mathcal G$ is \'{e}tale and both functions have compact support. Equivalently,
$$
A_R(\mathcal G)=\operatorname{span}_R\{\mathbf 1_U\mid U\in\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)\}.
$$
Moreover, for $U,V\in\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$,
$$
\mathbf 1_U\ast\mathbf 1_V=\mathbf 1_{UV}.
$$
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{unit-space-cut-downs}
Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be compact and open. For every $f\in A_R(\mathcal G)$ and every $\gamma\in\mathcal G$, one has
$$
(f\ast\mathbf 1_C)(\gamma)=f(\gamma)\mathbf 1_C(s(\gamma))
$$
and
$$
(\mathbf 1_C\ast f)(\gamma)=\mathbf 1_C(r(\gamma))f(\gamma).
$$
Consequently,
$$
A_R(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C=\{f\in A_R(\mathcal G)\mid\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq s^{-1}(C)\}
$$
and
$$
\mathbf 1_CA_R(\mathcal G)=\{f\in A_R(\mathcal G)\mid\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq r^{-1}(C)\}.
$$
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If $\beta\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$ and $\alpha\beta=\gamma$, then necessarily $\alpha=\gamma$ and $\beta=s(\gamma)$. Hence
$$
(f\ast\mathbf 1_C)(\gamma)=f(\gamma)\mathbf 1_C(s(\gamma)).
$$
The second identity is proved analogously. The two descriptions of the principal one-sided ideals follow immediately: for example, $f=f\ast\mathbf 1_C$ if and only if $f(\gamma)=0$ whenever $s(\gamma)\notin C$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{steinberg-local-units}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a Hausdorff ample groupoid, and let $R$ be a non-zero commutative unital ring. The family
$$
\{\mathbf 1_C\mid C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}\text{ is compact and open}\}
$$
is a set of local units for $A_R(\mathcal G)$. Furthermore, $A_R(\mathcal G)$ is unital if and only if $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is compact; in that case, its identity is $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal G^{(0)}}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $f_1,\dots,f_m\in A_R(\mathcal G)$. The set
$$
K=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\bigl(s(\operatorname{supp}(f_j))\cup r(\operatorname{supp}(f_j))\bigr)
$$
is compact in the unit space. Cover $K$ by finitely many compact open subsets of $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ and let $C$ be their union. Proposition~\ref{unit-space-cut-downs} gives
$$
\mathbf 1_C\ast f_j=f_j=f_j\ast\mathbf 1_C
$$
for every $j$. Also, $\mathbf 1_C\ast\mathbf 1_C=\mathbf 1_C$, so these idempotents are local units.

If $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is compact, the same cut-down formulas show that $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal G^{(0)}}$ is an identity. Conversely, suppose that $h\in A_R(\mathcal G)$ is an identity. For each $u\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$, choose a compact open neighborhood $C_u\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$. Then
$$
h(u)=(h\ast\mathbf 1_{C_u})(u)=\mathbf 1_{C_u}(u)=1_R\neq 0.
$$
Hence $\mathcal G^{(0)}\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(h)$. The unit space is closed in the Hausdorff groupoid: it is the equalizer of the continuous maps $\gamma\mapsto\gamma$ and $\gamma\mapsto s(\gamma)$, with the source regarded as a unit arrow. It follows that $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is a closed subset of the compact set $\operatorname{supp}(h)$ and is therefore compact.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a discrete group, regarded as a groupoid with one unit. Then every non-empty compact open bisection is a singleton $\{g\}$, with $g\in G$, and
$$
A_R(G)\cong RG.
$$
Under this identification, $\mathbf 1_{\{g\}}$ corresponds to the canonical basis element $g\in RG$. Thus Steinberg algebras genuinely extend ordinary group algebras.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The modern theory of groupoid amenability includes topological amenability, measurewise amenability, weak amenability, exactness and weak-containment phenomena for groupoid $C^*$-algebras and representations. We focus instead on the algebraic shadow of these notions in the setting of ample groupoids and Steinberg algebras; see \cite{ADR00,AnantharamanDelaroche23,Pacheco25,SridharanKumar26}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{algebraically-amenable-algebra}
Let $A$ be a $\Bbbk$-algebra, let $L\subseteq A$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. A non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A$ is called a \emph{left $(L,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace} if
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW) \leq (1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\frac{\dim_{\Bbbk}(\partial_L(W))}{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)} \leq \varepsilon.
$$
The algebra $A$ is called \emph{left algebraically amenable} if, for every finite-dimensional subspace $L\subseteq A$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, it admits a left $(L,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{proper-algebraic-amenability}
Elek's original definition for affine algebras requires an increasing exhaustive sequence of F{\o}lner subspaces; see \cite[Definition 1.1]{Elek03}. In the terminology of \cite[Definition 3.1 and Remark 3.3]{AraLiLledoWu18}, this is the stronger notion of \emph{proper algebraic amenability}. We do not impose exhaustivity in Definition~\ref{algebraically-amenable-algebra}. The distinction is essential for algebras with zero divisors: for example, the existence of a non-zero finite-dimensional left ideal already implies algebraic amenability, but need not imply proper algebraic amenability; see \cite[Example 3.7]{AraLiLledoWu18}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{unital-plus-W}
If $A$ is unital and $1_A\in L$, then $W\subseteq LW$, and hence
$$
W+LW=LW.
$$
We retain the term $+W$ because Steinberg algebras need not be unital when the unit space is non-compact. Although they have local units, as recalled in Section~\ref{preliminaries}, a fixed finite-dimensional test space $L$ need not contain a local unit for an arbitrary F{\o}lner subspace $W$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{generating-set-folner}
Let $A$ be a $\Bbbk$-algebra and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ satisfy
$$
A=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}(\Omega).
$$
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $A$ is left algebraically amenable;
    \item for every finite subset $\Omega_0\subseteq\Omega$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A$ such that
    $$
    \dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W\right)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W);
    $$
    \item for every finite subset $\Omega_0\subseteq\Omega$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A$ such that
    $$
    \dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\omega W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)
    $$
    for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Assume that $A$ is left algebraically amenable. Let $\Omega_0\subseteq\Omega$ be finite and let $\varepsilon>0$. Set
$$
L=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}(\Omega_0).
$$
Choose a left $(L,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace $W\subseteq A$. Since
$$
\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W\subseteq LW,
$$
we have
$$
W+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W\subseteq W+LW.
$$
Therefore
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W
\right)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
This proves $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$.

The implication $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$ is immediate, because for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$,
$$
W+\omega W\subseteq W+\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_0}\eta W.
$$

It remains to prove $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$. Let $L\subseteq A$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $\Omega$ linearly spans $A$, there exists a finite subset $\Omega_0\subseteq\Omega$ such that
$$
L\subseteq\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}(\Omega_0).
$$
Set $q=|\Omega_0|$. If $q=0$, then $L=\{0\}$. Since $A$ is non-zero, choose $0\neq a\in A$ and set
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{a\}.
$$
Then $W+LW=W$, so $W$ is a left $(L,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace.

Suppose now that $q\geq 1$. By condition $(3)$, applied with $\varepsilon/q$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A$ such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\omega W) \leq \left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{q}\right)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)
$$
for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$. Since
$$
W+LW \subseteq W+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W,
$$
it is enough to estimate the dimension of the latter space. Passing to the quotient by $W$ and using subadditivity of dimension gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W\right)-\dim_{\Bbbk}(W) \\
&\qquad= \dim_{\Bbbk}\left(\frac{W+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\omega W}{W}\right)\\
&\qquad\leq\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(\frac{W+\omega W}{W}\right)
\\
&\qquad=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_0}\left(\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\omega W)-\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)\right)
\\
&\qquad\leq q \frac{\varepsilon}{q}\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=\varepsilon\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
\end{aligned}
$$
Consequently,
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus $A$ is left algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{bartholdi-group-algebra}
Let $G$ be a discrete group and let $\Bbbk$ be a field. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $G$ is amenable;
    \item the group algebra $\Bbbk G$ is left algebraically amenable;
    \item the group algebra $\Bbbk G$ is right algebraically amenable.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Bartholdi proves the equivalence between amenability of $G$ and right algebraic amenability of $\Bbbk G$; see \cite[Definition 1.3 and Corollary 1.5]{Bartholdi08}. To pass between the right and left formulations, define
$$
\iota:\Bbbk G\longrightarrow\Bbbk G, \ \iota\left(\sum_{g\in G}\lambda_g g\right) = \sum_{g\in G}\lambda_g g^{-1}.
$$
The map $\iota$ is a $\Bbbk$-linear anti-automorphism, so
$$
\iota(ab)=\iota(b)\iota(a)
$$
for all $a,b\in\Bbbk G$.

Suppose that $\Bbbk G$ is right algebraically amenable. Let $L\subseteq\Bbbk G$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq\Bbbk G$ such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}\bigl(W+W\iota(L)\bigr) \leq (1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Since $\iota$ is a linear isomorphism and reverses products,
$$
\iota\bigl(W+W\iota(L)\bigr) = \iota(W)+L\iota(W).
$$
Therefore
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}\bigl(\iota(W)+L\iota(W)\bigr) \leq (1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}\bigl(\iota(W)\bigr),
$$
which proves left algebraic amenability. The reverse implication follows from the same argument because $\iota^2$ is the identity. Thus the left and right conditions are equivalent, and Bartholdi's result completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{weak-bisectional-folner}
Let $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ be finite and let $\varepsilon>0$. A non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ is called a \emph{weak $(\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace} if
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\mathbf 1_U W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)
$$
for every $U\in\mathcal E$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{weak-bisectional-amenability}
A Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called \emph{weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$} if, for every finite subset $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a weak $(\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{weak-bisectional-equivalence}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a Hausdorff ample groupoid. Then $\mathcal G$ is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$ if and only if its Steinberg algebra $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ is left algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Assume first that $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ is left algebraically amenable. Let $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ be finite and let $\varepsilon>0$. Set
$$
L=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_U\mid U\in\mathcal E\}.
$$
Choose a left $(L,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace $W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$. For every $U\in\mathcal E$,
$$
W+\mathbf 1_U W\subseteq W+LW.
$$
Hence
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\mathbf 1_U W)\leq\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus $W$ is a weak $(\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace.

Conversely, suppose that $\mathcal G$ is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable. Apply Lemma~\ref{generating-set-folner} to
$$
\Omega=\{\mathbf 1_U\mid U\in\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)\}.
$$
The family $\Omega$ spans $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$, and Definition~\ref{weak-bisectional-amenability} is precisely condition $(3)$ of that lemma. Therefore $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ is left algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{weak-condition-only-sees-algebra}
Proposition~\ref{weak-bisectional-equivalence} shows that weak bisectional amenability is exactly algebraic amenability of the Steinberg algebra expressed in its canonical bisection generators. It does not force the F{\o}lner subspace to interact with a prescribed region of the unit space. For groupoids with several components, this permits a F{\o}lner subspace to concentrate in only one component. The source-anchored condition introduced next prevents such avoidance when the prescribed anchor is contained in the unit space of that component. It does not, in general, prevent escape in the range direction.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{anchored-bisectional-folner}
Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ be finite and let $\varepsilon>0$. A non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
$$
is called a \emph{source-anchored $(C,\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace} if
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\mathbf 1_U W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)
$$
for every $U\in\mathcal E$.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
\label{anchored-algebraic-amenability}
A Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called \emph{source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$} if, for every non-empty compact open subset $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$, every finite subset $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a source-anchored $(C,\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{anchored-finite-dimensional-test}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a Hausdorff ample groupoid. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathcal G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$;
    \item for every non-empty compact open subset $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$, every finite-dimensional subspace $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
    $$
    W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
    $$
    such that
    $$
    \dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
    $$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Assume first that condition $(2)$ holds. Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ be finite and let $\varepsilon>0$. Set
$$
L=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_U\mid U\in\mathcal E\}.
$$
By condition $(2)$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
For every $U\in\mathcal E$,
$$
W+\mathbf 1_U W\subseteq W+LW.
$$
Therefore $W$ is a source-anchored $(C,\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace. Hence condition $(1)$ holds.

Conversely, assume condition $(1)$. Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Since the characteristic functions of compact open bisections linearly span $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$, there exists a finite subset $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ such that
$$
L\subseteq\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_U\mid U\in\mathcal E\}.
$$
Set $q=|\mathcal E|$. If $q=0$, then $L=\{0\}$. Taking
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_C\}\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
$$
gives $W+LW=W$.

Suppose that $q\geq 1$. By condition $(1)$, applied with $\varepsilon/q$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\mathbf 1_U W)\leq\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{q}\right)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)
$$
for every $U\in\mathcal E$. Since $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C$ is a left ideal, all spaces in the following computation remain inside that ideal. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{generating-set-folner},
$$
W+LW\subseteq W+\sum_{U\in\mathcal E}\mathbf 1_U W
$$
and
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\dim_{\Bbbk} \left(W+\sum_{U\in\mathcal E}\mathbf 1_U W\right)-\dim_{\Bbbk}(W) \\
&\qquad\leq\sum_{U\in\mathcal E}\left(\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+\mathbf 1_U W)-\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)\right) \\
&\qquad\leq q\frac{\varepsilon}{q}\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=\varepsilon\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
\end{aligned}
$$
Consequently,
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus condition $(2)$ holds.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{anchored-module-interpretation}
The source-anchored condition can be expressed in the language of algebraically amenable modules. For a non-zero left $A$-module $M$, use the left-handed analogue of \cite[Definition 1.3]{Bartholdi08}: for every finite-dimensional $L\subseteq A$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there must exist a non-zero finite-dimensional $W\subseteq M$ with
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
By Proposition~\ref{anchored-finite-dimensional-test}, a Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$ is source-anchored algebraically amenable exactly when every left module $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C$, with $C$ non-empty compact open in $\mathcal G^{(0)}$, has this property. Thus the anchoring selects a canonical family of modules determined by the unit space; the underlying module F{\o}lner condition is not a new notion of amenability for arbitrary algebras.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{anchored-implies-weak}
Every source-anchored left algebraically amenable Hausdorff ample groupoid is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal G$ be source-anchored left algebraically amenable. Since $\mathcal G$ is non-empty and ample, its unit space contains a non-empty compact open subset $C$. Given a finite subset $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, any source-anchored $(C,\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace is, after forgetting the containment in $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C$, a weak $(\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{weak-not-anchored}
The converse to Proposition~\ref{anchored-implies-weak} fails in general. As will be shown later, weak bisectional amenability may be witnessed inside a single amenable component even when another component is non-amenable. Source anchoring prevents this phenomenon by requiring a F{\o}lner subspace over every non-empty compact open region of the unit space.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{group-case}
Let $G$ be a countable discrete group and let $\Bbbk$ be a field. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $G$ is amenable;
    \item the group algebra $\Bbbk G$ is left algebraically amenable;
    \item the group algebra $\Bbbk G$ is right algebraically amenable;
    \item the one-unit groupoid associated to $G$ is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$;
    \item the one-unit groupoid associated to $G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The equivalence of conditions $(1)$--$(3)$ is Theorem~\ref{bartholdi-group-algebra}. The equivalence $(2)\Longleftrightarrow(4)$ follows from Proposition~\ref{weak-bisectional-equivalence}. Since the unit space consists of the single compact open set $\{e_G\}$ and
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(G)\mathbf 1_{\{e_G\}}=A_{\Bbbk}(G),
$$
conditions $(4)$ and $(5)$ are equivalent.

For completeness, we give the direct construction of the F{\o}lner subspaces in the implication $(1)\Rightarrow(5)$. Let $\mathcal E\subseteq\operatorname{Bis}_c(G)$ be finite and let $\varepsilon>0$. Discarding the empty bisection, there is a finite subset $K\subseteq G$ such that
$$
\mathcal E\setminus\{\varnothing\}=\{\{g\}\mid g\in K\}.
$$
Apply the left F{\o}lner condition to $K^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon$. There exists a non-empty finite subset $F\subseteq G$ such that
$$
\frac{|F\setminus g^{-1}F|}{|F|}<\varepsilon
$$
for every $g\in K$. Since left multiplication by $g$ is a bijection,
$$
|gF\setminus F|=|F\setminus g^{-1}F|.
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{|F\cup gF|}{|F|}=1+\frac{|gF\setminus F|}{|F|}<1+\varepsilon
$$
for every $g\in K$.

Define
$$
W_F=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\delta_t\mid t\in F\}\subseteq\Bbbk G.
$$
The canonical group elements $\{\delta_t\mid t\in G\}$ form a $\Bbbk$-basis of $\Bbbk G$, and
$$
\delta_g W_F=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\delta_{gt}\mid t\in F\}.
$$
Consequently,
$$
W_F+\delta_g W_F=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\delta_t\mid t\in F\cup gF\},
$$
and hence
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_F+\delta_g W_F)&=|F\cup gF|\\
&<(1+\varepsilon)|F|\\
&=(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_F).
\end{aligned}
$$
For the empty bisection, multiplication by $\mathbf 1_{\varnothing}=0$ leaves $W_F$ unchanged. Finally,
$$
W_F\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(G)\mathbf 1_{\{e_G\}}=A_{\Bbbk}(G),
$$
so $W_F$ is a source-anchored $(\{e_G\},\mathcal E,\varepsilon)$-bisectional F{\o}lner subspace.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{field-independence-group-case}
Let $G$ be a countable discrete group. If the one-unit groupoid associated to $G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over one field, then it is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over every field.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, source-anchored algebraic amenability over one field is equivalent to amenability of $G$, and amenability of $G$ is independent of the coefficient field. Applying the same theorem to any other field gives the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{group-case} is the basic consistency test for the groupoid notion developed here. It shows that source anchoring introduces no additional restriction in the one-unit setting, while for groupoids with many units it prevents F{\o}lner subspaces from avoiding prescribed compact open regions of the unit space.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{isomorphism-invariance}
Let $\Phi:\mathcal G\longrightarrow\mathcal H$ be an isomorphism of topological groupoids between Hausdorff ample groupoids. Then $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$ if and only if $\mathcal H$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The groupoid isomorphism $\Phi$ induces a $\Bbbk$-algebra isomorphism
$$
\Phi_{\#}:A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G) \longrightarrow A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H), \ \Phi_{\#}(f)=f\circ\Phi^{-1}.
$$
For every compact open bisection $U\subseteq\mathcal G$,
$$
\Phi_{\#}(\mathbf 1_U)=\mathbf 1_{\Phi(U)}.
$$
In particular, if $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is compact and open, then
$$
\Phi_{\#}\left(A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C\right)= A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_{\Phi(C)}.
$$
Moreover, $\Phi_{\#}$ preserves products, finite-dimensionality and vector-space dimension. Therefore, the image under $\Phi_{\#}$ of a source-anchored F{\o}lner subspace for $(C,L,\varepsilon)$ is a source-anchored F{\o}lner subspace for
$$
\left(\Phi(C),\Phi_{\#}(L),\varepsilon\right).
$$
Applying the same argument to $\Phi^{-1}$ proves the converse.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{source-saturated-subgroupoid}
Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$ be a subgroupoid and put $Y=\mathcal H^{(0)}$. We say that $\mathcal H$ is \emph{source-saturated in $\mathcal G$} if
$$
s_{\mathcal G}^{-1}(Y)\subseteq\mathcal H.
$$
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{source-saturated-reduction}
Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$ be a subgroupoid and put $Y=\mathcal H^{(0)}$. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathcal H$ is source-saturated in $\mathcal G$;
    \item $Y$ is invariant in $\mathcal G$ and
    $$
    \mathcal H=\mathcal G|_Y.
    $$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Assume first that $\mathcal H$ is source-saturated. Let $\gamma\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $s(\gamma)\in Y$. Then $\gamma\in\mathcal H$, and hence $r(\gamma)\in\mathcal H^{(0)}=Y$. Conversely, if $r(\gamma)\in Y$, then
$$
s(\gamma^{-1})=r(\gamma)\in Y.
$$
Source saturation gives $\gamma^{-1}\in\mathcal H$, and therefore $\gamma\in\mathcal H$ and $s(\gamma)\in Y$. Thus
$$
s(\gamma)\in Y\ \Longleftrightarrow\ r(\gamma)\in Y,
$$
so $Y$ is invariant.

Every arrow of $\mathcal H$ has source and range in $Y$, and hence
$$
\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G|_Y.
$$
Conversely, if $\gamma\in\mathcal G|_Y$, then $s(\gamma)\in Y$, so source saturation implies $\gamma\in\mathcal H$. Therefore
$$
\mathcal H=\mathcal G|_Y.
$$

The converse is immediate. If $Y$ is invariant and $\mathcal H=\mathcal G|_Y$, then every $\gamma\in\mathcal G$ with $s(\gamma)\in Y$ also satisfies $r(\gamma)\in Y$, and hence $\gamma\in\mathcal G|_Y=\mathcal H$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{open-subgroupoid-extension-by-zero}
Let $\mathcal H$ be an open subgroupoid of a Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$, equipped with the subspace topology. Extension by zero defines an injective algebra homomorphism
$$
j:A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\longrightarrow A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G).
$$
If $Y=\mathcal H^{(0)}$ is invariant in $\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal H=\mathcal G|_Y$, then, for every compact open $C\subseteq Y$,
$$
j\bigl(A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_C\bigr)=A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C.
$$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For $f\in A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)$, define $j(f)$ to agree with $f$ on $\mathcal H$ and to vanish elsewhere. Its support is compact in $\mathcal G$, since the inclusion of $\mathcal H$ is continuous. It is also closed in $\mathcal G$, since $\mathcal G$ is Hausdorff. Local constancy holds on the open set $\mathcal H$, and every point outside $\mathcal H$ has an open neighborhood disjoint from this support. Thus $j(f)$ is locally constant and compactly supported.

A non-zero summand in $(j(f)\ast j(g))(\gamma)$ has both factors in $\mathcal H$. Their product belongs to $\mathcal H$, since $\mathcal H$ is a subgroupoid. For $\gamma\in\mathcal H$, the remaining summands are exactly those defining $(f\ast g)(\gamma)$; for $\gamma\notin\mathcal H$, there are none. Hence $j(f)\ast j(g)=j(f\ast g)$. Linearity and injectivity are immediate.

Under the additional hypotheses, every arrow with source in $C$ has range in $Y$ and therefore belongs to $\mathcal H$. Proposition~\ref{unit-space-cut-downs} gives the asserted equality of left ideals. For the reverse inclusion in that equality, restriction of a function supported in $s^{-1}(C)$ to $\mathcal H$ remains locally constant and compactly supported.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{open-invariant-reduction}
Let $\mathcal G$ be an algebraically amenable Hausdorff ample groupoid, and let $Y\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, open and invariant. Then the reduction $\mathcal G|_Y$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Set
$$
\mathcal H=\mathcal G|_Y.
$$
Since $Y$ is open and invariant, $\mathcal H$ is an open Hausdorff ample subgroupoid of $\mathcal G$. Extension by zero identifies $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)$ with a subalgebra of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathcal H^{(0)}=Y$ be non-empty, compact and open in $Y$. Because $Y$ is open in $\mathcal G^{(0)}$, the set $C$ is also open in $\mathcal G^{(0)}$. It is compact in $\mathcal G^{(0)}$ because the inclusion $Y\hookrightarrow\mathcal G^{(0)}$ is continuous. Hence $C$ is a non-empty compact open subset of $\mathcal G^{(0)}$.

Let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. We regard $L$ as a subspace of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ by extension by zero. Since $Y$ is invariant and $C\subseteq Y$, every arrow of $\mathcal G$ with source in $C$ belongs to $\mathcal H$. Consequently,
$$
s_{\mathcal G}^{-1}(C)=s_{\mathcal H}^{-1}(C).
$$
Using Proposition~\ref{unit-space-cut-downs}, we obtain
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C=A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_C.
$$

Since $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable, Proposition~\ref{anchored-finite-dimensional-test} gives a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
The equality of the anchored ideals shows that
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_C.
$$
Thus the same subspace $W$ verifies the source-anchored F{\o}lner condition for $\mathcal H$. Therefore $\mathcal H$ is algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{source-saturated-subgroupoid-col}
Let $\mathcal H$ be a non-empty open source-saturated subgroupoid of an algebraically amenable Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$. Then $\mathcal H$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{source-saturated-reduction}, there is an open invariant subset $Y\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ such that
$$
\mathcal H=\mathcal G|_Y.
$$
The conclusion follows from Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{weak-not-anchored-counterexample}
There exists a Hausdorff ample groupoid that is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$ but is not source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $F_2$ be the free group on two generators, regarded as a one-unit discrete groupoid, and let $\mathcal T$ be the trivial groupoid with one unit $u$. Consider the topological disjoint union
$$
\mathcal G=F_2\sqcup\mathcal T.
$$
This is a Hausdorff ample groupoid.

Set
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}\}.
$$
Let $U\in\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$. The intersection $U\cap\mathcal T$ is either empty or equal to $\{u\}$. Hence
$$
\mathbf 1_UW=\begin{cases}\{0\}, & U\cap\mathcal T=\varnothing,\\ W, & U\cap\mathcal T=\{u\}.\end{cases}
$$
Therefore
$$
W+\mathbf 1_UW=W
$$
for every $U\in\operatorname{Bis}_c(\mathcal G)$. The same one-dimensional subspace works for every finite family of compact open bisections and every $\varepsilon>0$. Thus $\mathcal G$ is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that $\mathcal G$ were source-anchored left algebraically amenable. The unit space of the $F_2$-component is an open invariant subset of $\mathcal G^{(0)}$. Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction} would imply that the reduction to this component, namely the one-unit groupoid $F_2$, is source-anchored left algebraically amenable. By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, this would imply that $F_2$ is an amenable group, contradicting the classical non-amenability of $F_2$. Hence $\mathcal G$ is not source-anchored left algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{arbitrary-subgroupoids-fail}
Source-anchored left algebraic amenability is not inherited by arbitrary Hausdorff ample subgroupoids. In fact, there exists a countable discrete algebraically amenable groupoid containing an open subgroupoid isomorphic to the non-amenable group $F_2$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $I=\mathbb N$ and let $\Gamma=F_2$. Consider the discrete groupoid
$$
\mathcal G=I\times\Gamma\times I.
$$
Its unit space is identified with $I$ through
$$
i\longleftrightarrow(i,e_{\Gamma},i).
$$
The range and source maps are
$$
r(i,g,j)=i, \ s(i,g,j)=j,
$$
and the multiplication and inversion are given by
$$
(i,g,j)(j,h,k)=(i,gh,k) \text{ and }(i,g,j)^{-1}=(j,g^{-1},i).
$$
Since $\mathcal G$ is discrete, it is Hausdorff and ample, and every compact subset of $\mathcal G$ is finite.

We first prove that $\mathcal G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable. Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}=I$ be non-empty, compact and open. Thus $C$ is a non-empty finite subset of $I$. Let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$.

Choose a basis $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $L$, where the list is allowed to be empty when $L=\{0\}$. Since every $f_j$ has finite support, the set
$$
S=\bigcup_{j=1}^n\operatorname{supp}(f_j)
$$
is finite. Hence
$$
s(S)=\{s(\alpha)\mid\alpha\in S\}
$$
is a finite subset of $I$. Choose
$$
i_0\in I\setminus s(S)
$$
and choose $c_0\in C$. Set
$$
\beta=(i_0,e_{\Gamma},c_0)
$$
and
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_{\{\beta\}}\}.
$$
Because $s(\beta)=c_0\in C$, Proposition~\ref{unit-space-cut-downs} gives
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C.
$$

We claim that $LW=\{0\}$. Indeed, if $\alpha\in S$, then the product $\alpha\beta$ can be defined only if
$$
s(\alpha)=r(\beta)=i_0.
$$
This is impossible because $i_0\notin s(S)$. Therefore
$$
f_j\ast\mathbf 1_{\{\beta\}}=0
$$
for every $j$, and hence $LW=\{0\}$. It follows that
$$
W+LW=W
$$
and consequently
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus $\mathcal G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable.

Fix $u\in I$ and consider the isotropy subgroupoid
$$
\mathcal H=\{u\}\times\Gamma\times\{u\}.
$$
Since $\mathcal G$ is discrete, $\mathcal H$ is an open Hausdorff ample subgroupoid. It is a one-unit groupoid naturally isomorphic to $\Gamma=F_2$. By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable if and only if $F_2$ is amenable. Since $F_2$ is not amenable, $\mathcal H$ is not source-anchored left algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{range-escape}
Proposition~\ref{arbitrary-subgroupoids-fail} shows precisely what source anchoring controls. The condition
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C
$$
forces the source of the support of $W$ to lie in $C$, but it does not constrain its range. In the preceding example, the vector $\mathbf 1_{\{\beta\}}$ starts at $c_0\in C$ and ends at a unit $i_0$ outside the finite source set detected by $L$. This \emph{range escape} makes the F{\o}lner boundary vanish. An arbitrary subgroupoid need not contain the escaping arrow $\beta$. By contrast, an open invariant reduction contains every arrow whose source belongs to its unit space, which is exactly why Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction} holds.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{one-unit-permanence}
Within the class of countable one-unit groupoids, source-anchored left algebraic amenability is preserved under the following operations:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item passing to subgroupoids induced by subgroups;
    \item passing to quotient groups;
    \item taking extensions by amenable normal subgroups;
    \item taking finite direct products;
    \item taking directed unions of subgroups;
    \item taking countable direct sums of groups.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, a countable one-unit groupoid is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$ exactly when its underlying group is amenable. Each assertion therefore follows from the corresponding classical permanence property for amenable groups recalled in Section~\ref{preliminaries}. For the direct-sum statement, every finitely generated subgroup of a countable direct sum is contained in a finite direct product of the coordinate groups; finite products and subgroups of amenable groups are amenable.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{disjoint-unions}
Let $(\mathcal G_i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family of Hausdorff ample groupoids, and let
$$
\mathcal G=\bigsqcup_{i\in I}\mathcal G_i
$$
be their topological disjoint union. Then $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$ if and only if every $\mathcal G_i$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Assume first that $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable. For each $i\in I$, the unit space $\mathcal G_i^{(0)}$ is an open invariant subset of $\mathcal G^{(0)}$, and
$$
\mathcal G|_{\mathcal G_i^{(0)}}=\mathcal G_i.
$$
Therefore Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction} implies that every $\mathcal G_i$ is algebraically amenable.

Conversely, suppose that every $\mathcal G_i$ is algebraically amenable. Since a compact subset of a topological disjoint union meets only finitely many components, extension by zero yields an algebraic direct-sum decomposition
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)=\bigoplus_{i\in I}A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_i).
$$
Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$.

Choose $i_0\in I$ such that
$$
C_{i_0}=C\cap\mathcal G_{i_0}^{(0)}
$$
is non-empty. The component $\mathcal G_{i_0}^{(0)}$ is clopen in $\mathcal G^{(0)}$, so $C_{i_0}$ is compact and open in $\mathcal G_{i_0}^{(0)}$. Let
$$
\pi_{i_0}:A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\longrightarrow A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_{i_0})
$$
be the coordinate projection, and put
$$
L_{i_0}=\pi_{i_0}(L).
$$
Since $\mathcal G_{i_0}$ is algebraically amenable, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_{i_0})\mathbf 1_{C_{i_0}}
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+L_{i_0}W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$

We regard $W$ as a subspace of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ by extension by zero. Since there are no composable arrows belonging to different components, one has
$$
aW=\pi_{i_0}(a)W
$$
for every $a\in A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$. Consequently,
$$
LW=L_{i_0}W.
$$
Moreover, $C_{i_0}\subseteq C$ implies
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C.
$$
Therefore
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+L_{i_0}W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{products}
Let $\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal H$ be Hausdorff ample groupoids. If both are algebraically amenable, then $\mathcal G\times\mathcal H$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The product $\mathcal G\times\mathcal H$ is again a Hausdorff ample groupoid. By the tensor-product theorem for Steinberg algebras, there is a natural $\Bbbk$-algebra isomorphism
$$
\Theta:A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\otimes_{\Bbbk}A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\longrightarrow A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G\times\mathcal H)
$$
satisfying
$$
\Theta(f\otimes g)(\gamma,\eta)=f(\gamma)g(\eta);
$$
see \cite[Theorem 4.3]{Rigby21}. In particular,
$$
\Theta(\mathbf 1_U\otimes\mathbf 1_V)=\mathbf 1_{U\times V}
$$
for compact open bisections $U\subseteq\mathcal G$ and $V\subseteq\mathcal H$. We use $\Theta$ to identify the two algebras.

Let
$$
C\subseteq(\mathcal G\times\mathcal H)^{(0)}=\mathcal G^{(0)}\times\mathcal H^{(0)}
$$
be non-empty, compact and open. Choose a point $(x,y)\in C$. Since both unit spaces have bases of compact open subsets, there exist non-empty compact open subsets
$$
C_{\mathcal G}\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}, \ C_{\mathcal H}\subseteq\mathcal H^{(0)}
$$
such that
$$
(x,y)\in C_{\mathcal G}\times C_{\mathcal H}\subseteq C.
$$

Let
$$
L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\otimes_{\Bbbk}A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)
$$
be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a basis $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ of $L$. Write each basis vector as a finite sum of elementary tensors,
$$
\ell_j=\sum_{r=1}^{m_j}a_{j,r}\otimes b_{j,r}.
$$
Set
$$
L_{\mathcal G}=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{a_{j,r}\mid 1\leq j\leq n,\ 1\leq r\leq m_j\}
$$
and
$$
L_{\mathcal H}=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{b_{j,r}\mid 1\leq j\leq n,\ 1\leq r\leq m_j\}.
$$
Then
$$
L\subseteq L_{\mathcal G}\otimes_{\Bbbk}L_{\mathcal H}.
$$
Choose
$$
\delta=\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}-1>0,
$$
so that
$$
(1+\delta)^2=1+\varepsilon.
$$

By algebraic amenability of $\mathcal G$, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W_{\mathcal G}\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_{C_{\mathcal G}}
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W_{\mathcal G}+L_{\mathcal G}W_{\mathcal G}\right)\leq(1+\delta)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_{\mathcal G}).
$$
Similarly, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W_{\mathcal H}\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_{C_{\mathcal H}}
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W_{\mathcal H}+L_{\mathcal H}W_{\mathcal H}\right)\leq(1+\delta)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_{\mathcal H}).
$$

Define
$$
W=W_{\mathcal G}\otimes_{\Bbbk}W_{\mathcal H}.
$$
Then $W$ is non-zero and finite-dimensional. Moreover,
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G\times\mathcal H) \mathbf 1_{C_{\mathcal G}\times C_{\mathcal H}}.
$$
Since $C_{\mathcal G}\times C_{\mathcal H}\subseteq C$, one has
$$
\mathbf 1_{C_{\mathcal G}\times C_{\mathcal H}}\ast\mathbf 1_C=\mathbf 1_{C_{\mathcal G}\times C_{\mathcal H}},
$$
and therefore
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G\times\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_C.
$$

Since $L\subseteq L_{\mathcal G}\otimes L_{\mathcal H}$,
$$
LW\subseteq(L_{\mathcal G}W_{\mathcal G})\otimes_{\Bbbk}(L_{\mathcal H}W_{\mathcal H}).
$$
Hence
$$
W+LW\subseteq\left(W_{\mathcal G}+L_{\mathcal G}W_{\mathcal G}\right)\otimes_{\Bbbk}\left(W_{\mathcal H}+L_{\mathcal H}W_{\mathcal H}\right).
$$
Taking dimensions gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW) &\leq\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W_{\mathcal G}+L_{\mathcal G}W_{\mathcal G}\right)\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W_{\mathcal H}+L_{\mathcal H}W_{\mathcal H}\right)\\
&\leq(1+\delta)^2\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_{\mathcal G})\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_{\mathcal H})\\
&=(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus $\mathcal G\times\mathcal H$ is algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{finite-products}
Every finite product of algebraically amenable Hausdorff ample groupoids is algebraically amenable.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{products} inductively.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{directed-unions}
Let $(\mathcal G_i)_{i\in I}$ be a directed family, under inclusion, of open Hausdorff ample subgroupoids of a Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$. Suppose that
$$
\mathcal G=\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal G_i
$$
and that every $\mathcal G_i$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$. Then $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a basis $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $L$, allowing the list to be empty if $L=\{0\}$. The set
$$
K=C\cup\bigcup_{j=1}^n\operatorname{supp}(f_j)
$$
is compact in $\mathcal G$.

The family $(\mathcal G_i)_{i\in I}$ is an open cover of $\mathcal G$, so finitely many members cover $K$. Directedness gives an index $i_0\in I$ containing all those finitely many subgroupoids. Hence
$$
K\subseteq\mathcal G_{i_0}.
$$
In particular,
$$
C\subseteq\mathcal G_{i_0}^{(0)} \text{ and } L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_{i_0}),
$$
where the latter algebra is viewed inside $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ by extension by zero. Since $\mathcal G_{i_0}$ is open, the set $C$ is compact and open in $\mathcal G_{i_0}^{(0)}$.

Algebraic amenability of $\mathcal G_{i_0}$ yields a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_{i_0})\mathbf 1_C
$$
such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
After extension by zero,
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C,
$$
and the same multiplication and the same dimension estimate hold in $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$. Therefore $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{locally-finite-dimensional-steinberg}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a Hausdorff ample groupoid. Suppose that every finite subset of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ is contained in a finite-dimensional $\Bbbk$-subalgebra of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$. Then $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $C\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a basis $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ of $L$. By hypothesis, there exists a finite-dimensional subalgebra
$$
B\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)
$$
containing
$$
\{\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n,\mathbf 1_C\}.
$$
Set
$$
W=B\mathbf 1_C.
$$
The space $W$ is finite-dimensional and
$$
\mathbf 1_C=\mathbf 1_C\ast\mathbf 1_C\in W,
$$
so $W\neq\{0\}$. Also,
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)\mathbf 1_C.
$$
Since $L\subseteq B$ and $B$ is a subalgebra,
$$
LW=L(B\mathbf 1_C)\subseteq B\mathbf 1_C=W.
$$
Therefore
$$
W+LW=W
$$
and
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{finite-dimensional-steinberg}
If $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ is finite-dimensional, then $\mathcal G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{locally-finite-dimensional-steinberg} with the finite-dimensional subalgebra $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G)$ itself.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{af-groupoid-definition}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a second-countable Hausdorff ample groupoid with compact unit space. An open subgroupoid $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$ is called \emph{elementary} if $\mathcal H$ is compact and principal and
$$
\mathcal H^{(0)}=\mathcal G^{(0)}.
$$
The groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called an \emph{AF groupoid} if there exists an increasing sequence
$$
\mathcal H_1\subseteq\mathcal H_2\subseteq\cdots
$$
of elementary subgroupoids such that
$$
\mathcal G=\bigcup_{n\geq 1}\mathcal H_n.
$$
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{af-groupoids}
Every AF groupoid is algebraically amenable over every field $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
For an AF groupoid, the Steinberg algebra over a field is ultramatricial; see \cite[\S 5]{ClarkHazrat20}. In particular, it is a directed union of finite-dimensional subalgebras, so every finite subset is contained in a finite-dimensional subalgebra. Proposition~\ref{locally-finite-dimensional-steinberg} gives the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{infinite-transitive-discrete-groupoid}
Let $\mathcal H$ be a countable transitive discrete groupoid whose unit space $\mathcal H^{(0)}$ is infinite. Then $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over every field $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let $C\subseteq\mathcal H^{(0)}$ be non-empty, compact and open, let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $\mathcal H^{(0)}$ is discrete, the compact set $C$ is finite.

Choose a basis $f_1,\dots,f_m$ of $L$ and put
$$
S=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\operatorname{supp}(f_j).
$$
Every $f_j$ has finite support because $\mathcal H$ is discrete and $f_j$ is compactly supported. Hence $S$ and $s(S)$ are finite. Since $\mathcal H^{(0)}$ is infinite, there exists
$$
v\in\mathcal H^{(0)}\setminus s(S).
$$
Choose $c\in C$. By transitivity, there is an arrow $\beta\in\mathcal H$ such that
$$
s(\beta)=c,\ r(\beta)=v.
$$
Define
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_{\{\beta\}}\}.
$$
Since $s(\beta)=c\in C$, Proposition~\ref{unit-space-cut-downs} gives
$$
W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_C.
$$

We claim that $LW=\{0\}$. Indeed, let $f\in L$. Every arrow in $\operatorname{supp}(f)$ belongs to $S$. A product $\alpha\beta$ can be defined only if
$$
s(\alpha)=r(\beta)=v.
$$
However, $v\notin s(S)$, so no arrow $\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(f)$ is composable on the left with $\beta$. Consequently,
$$
f\ast\mathbf 1_{\{\beta\}}=0.
$$
Since this holds for every $f\in L$, we obtain $LW=\{0\}$. Therefore
$$
W+LW=W,
$$
and hence
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Thus $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$. Since the argument does not depend on the field, the conclusion holds over every field.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{finite-transitive-matrix-model}
Let $\mathcal H$ be a transitive discrete groupoid with finite unit space
$$
O=\mathcal H^{(0)}=\{u_1,\dots,u_n\}.
$$
Fix $u=u_1$ and put
$$
K=\mathcal H_u^u.
$$
For each $1\leq i\leq n$, choose an arrow $\tau_i\in\mathcal H$ such that
$$
s(\tau_i)=u,\ r(\tau_i)=u_i,
$$
and take $\tau_1=u$. Then the map
$$
\Psi:O\times K\times O\longrightarrow\mathcal H, \ \Psi(u_i,k,u_j)=\tau_i k\tau_j^{-1},
$$
is a groupoid isomorphism. Moreover, for every field $\Bbbk$, it induces a $\Bbbk$-algebra isomorphism
$$
\Phi:A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\longrightarrow M_n(\Bbbk K)
$$
determined by
$$
\Phi\left(\mathbf 1_{\{\tau_i k\tau_j^{-1}\}}\right)=e_{ij}(k),
$$
where $e_{ij}(k)$ denotes the matrix whose $(i,j)$-entry is $k$ and whose other entries are zero. In particular,
$$
\Phi\left(\mathbf 1_{\{u_i\}}\right)=e_{ii}(1_{\Bbbk K})
$$
and
$$
\Phi\left(A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_{\{u_j\}}\right)=M_n(\Bbbk K)e_{jj}(1_{\Bbbk K}).
$$
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $\gamma\in\mathcal H$ satisfy
$$
s(\gamma)=u_j,\ r(\gamma)=u_i.
$$
Then
$$
k_{\gamma}=\tau_i^{-1}\gamma\tau_j
$$
is an arrow from $u$ to $u$, and therefore $k_{\gamma}\in K$. Moreover,
$$
\gamma=\tau_i k_{\gamma}\tau_j^{-1}.
$$
This expression is unique: if
$$
\tau_i k\tau_j^{-1}=\tau_i \ell\tau_j^{-1},
$$
then multiplication on the left by $\tau_i^{-1}$ and on the right by $\tau_j$ gives $k=\ell$. Hence $\Psi$ is bijective.

The element $(u_i,k,u_j)$ has source $u_j$ and range $u_i$. If $u_j=u_p$, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Psi(u_i,k,u_j)\Psi(u_p,\ell,u_q)&=
\tau_i k\tau_j^{-1}\tau_j\ell\tau_q^{-1} \\
&= \tau_i k\ell\tau_q^{-1} \\
&= \Psi(u_i,k\ell,u_q).
\end{aligned}
$$
Also,
$$
\Psi(u_i,k,u_j)^{-1}= \tau_j k^{-1}\tau_i^{-1} = \Psi(u_j,k^{-1},u_i).
$$
Thus $\Psi$ preserves source, range, multiplication, inversion and units. Since both groupoids are discrete, it is an isomorphism of topological groupoids.

The Steinberg algebra of a discrete groupoid is the algebra of finitely supported $\Bbbk$-valued functions on its arrow space. The singleton characteristic functions form a $\Bbbk$-basis. For $a,b\in\Bbbk K$, let $e_{ij}(a)$ denote the matrix with $a$ in the $(i,j)$-entry and zero elsewhere. Then
$$
e_{ij}(a)e_{pq}(b)=\begin{cases}
 e_{iq}(ab), & j=p,\\
 0, & j\neq p.
\end{cases}
$$
On the groupoid side,
$$
\mathbf 1_{\{\tau_i k\tau_j^{-1}\}}\ast\mathbf 1_{\{\tau_p\ell\tau_q^{-1}\}}=\begin{cases}
\mathbf 1_{\{\tau_i k\ell\tau_q^{-1}\}}, & j=p,\\
0, & j\neq p.
\end{cases}
$$
Therefore the displayed assignment extends uniquely to a multiplicative $\Bbbk$-linear bijection
$$
\Phi:A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\longrightarrow M_n(\Bbbk K).
$$
Finally, the unit $u_i$ corresponds to the arrow $\tau_i1_K\tau_i^{-1}$, so
$$
\Phi(\mathbf 1_{\{u_i\}})=e_{ii}(1_{\Bbbk K}).
$$
Since $\Phi$ is multiplicative, it maps the left ideal generated by $\mathbf 1_{\{u_j\}}$ onto the left ideal generated by $e_{jj}(1_{\Bbbk K})$. This proves the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{finite-transitive-isotropy}
Let $\mathcal H$ be a countable transitive discrete groupoid with finite non-empty unit space, let $u\in\mathcal H^{(0)}$, and put
$$
K=\mathcal H_u^u.
$$
Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$;
    \item the isotropy group $K$ is amenable;
    \item every isotropy group of $\mathcal H$ is amenable.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over one field, then it is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over every field.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Write
$$
\mathcal H^{(0)}=\{u_1,\dots,u_n\},\ u_1=u,
$$
and use Lemma~\ref{finite-transitive-matrix-model} to identify
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\cong M_n(R), \ R=\Bbbk K.
$$
Under this identification, $\mathbf 1_{\{u_i\}}$ corresponds to $e_{ii}(1_R)$.

We first prove $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$. Assume that $K$ is amenable. By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, the group algebra $R=\Bbbk K$ is left algebraically amenable.

Let $C\subseteq\mathcal H^{(0)}$ be non-empty, let
$$
L\subseteq M_n(R)
$$
be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Since the unit space is finite and discrete, $C$ is compact and open. Choose $u_\ell\in C$. Choose a basis
$$
A^{(1)},\dots,A^{(m)}
$$
of $L$, and let $E\subseteq R$ be the finite-dimensional subspace spanned by $1_R$ and all matrix entries of the matrices $A^{(1)},\dots,A^{(m)}$. Then every entry of every matrix in $L$ belongs to $E$.

Since $R$ is left algebraically amenable, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $V\subseteq R$ such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(V+EV)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$
Because $1_R\in E$, one has $V\subseteq EV$, and consequently
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$

Define
$$
W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n e_{i\ell}(V),
$$
where
$$
e_{i\ell}(V)=\{e_{i\ell}(v)\mid v\in V\}.
$$
Thus $W$ consists of the matrices supported in the $\ell$-th column whose entries belong to $V$. It is non-zero and finite-dimensional, and
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=n\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$
Moreover,
$$
W\subseteq M_n(R)e_{\ell\ell}(1_R)\subseteq M_n(R)\sum_{u_i\in C}e_{ii}(1_R).
$$
Hence, under the inverse of $\Phi$, the space $W$ is contained in
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal H)\mathbf 1_C.
$$

Let $A=(a_{ij})\in L$ and let
$$
w=\sum_{j=1}^n e_{j\ell}(v_j)\in W.
$$
The product $Aw$ is supported in the $\ell$-th column, and its $(i,\ell)$-entry is
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}v_j.
$$
Since $a_{ij}\in E$ and $v_j\in V$, this entry belongs to $EV$. Therefore
$$
LW\subseteq\bigoplus_{i=1}^n e_{i\ell}(EV).
$$
Because $V\subseteq EV$, the same ambient space also contains $W$. It follows that
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)
&\leq
n\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV)
\\
&\leq
(1+\varepsilon)n\dim_{\Bbbk}(V)
\\
&=
(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.

We now prove $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$. Assume that $\mathcal H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$. Let $E_0\subseteq R$ be finite-dimensional and let $\varepsilon>0$. Put
$$
E=E_0+\Bbbk 1_R
$$
and define the finite-dimensional subspace
$$
M_n(E)=\{(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)\mid a_{ij}\in E\}.
$$
Apply source-anchored algebraic amenability to the compact open singleton $\{u_1\}$ and to the multiplier space $M_n(E)$. We obtain a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace
$$
W\subseteq M_n(R)e_{11}(1_R)
$$
such that
$$\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W+M_n(E)W\right)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$

Identify the left ideal $M_n(R)e_{11}(1_R)$ with the column space $R^n$. For $1\leq i\leq n$, let
$$
\pi_i:R^n\longrightarrow R
$$
be the $i$-th coordinate projection, and put
$$
V=\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i(W).
$$
The space $V$ is finite-dimensional. It is non-zero because $W\neq\{0\}$.

We claim that
$$
M_n(E)W=(EV)^n.
$$
For the inclusion from left to right, let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(E)$ and $w=(w_1,\dots,w_n)^{\mathsf T}\in W$. The $i$-th coordinate of $Aw$ is
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}w_j,
$$
which belongs to $EV$ because $a_{ij}\in E$ and $w_j\in\pi_j(W)\subseteq V$. Thus
$$
M_n(E)W\subseteq(EV)^n.
$$

For the reverse inclusion, let $a\in E$, let $w\in W$, and fix indices $i$ and $j$. Multiplication by the elementary matrix $e_{ij}(a)\in M_n(E)$ produces a column vector whose $i$-th coordinate is $a\pi_j(w)$ and whose other coordinates are zero. Since
$$
V=\sum_{j=1}^n\pi_j(W),
$$
the vectors $a\pi_j(w)$ span $EV$ when $a$, $j$ and $w$ vary. Therefore every column vector having one prescribed coordinate in $EV$ and all other coordinates equal to zero belongs to $M_n(E)W$. Summing over the coordinates gives
$$
(EV)^n\subseteq M_n(E)W.
$$
This proves the claim.

Since $1_R\in E$, we have $V\subseteq EV$. Moreover,
$$
W\subseteq V^n\subseteq(EV)^n=M_n(E)W.
$$
Hence
$$
W+M_n(E)W=M_n(E)W=(EV)^n.
$$
It follows that
$$
\begin{aligned}
n\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV)&=\dim_{\Bbbk}\left(W+M_n(E)W\right)\\
&\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W) \\
&\leq(1+\varepsilon)n\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
\end{aligned}
$$
After cancelling $n$, we obtain
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$
Finally, since $1_R\in E$ and $E_0\subseteq E$,
$$
V+E_0V\subseteq EV.
$$
Therefore
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(V+E_0V)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$
Thus $R=\Bbbk K$ is left algebraically amenable. By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, the group $K$ is amenable. This proves $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$.

For every $x\in\mathcal H^{(0)}$, choose an arrow $\gamma\in\mathcal H$ with
$$
s(\gamma)=u,\ r(\gamma)=x.
$$
Conjugation by $\gamma$ gives a group isomorphism
$$
K\longrightarrow\mathcal H_x^x, \ k\longmapsto\gamma k\gamma^{-1}.
$$
Hence $(2)$ and $(3)$ are equivalent.

Finally, condition~$(2)$ is independent of the coefficient field. If condition~$(1)$ holds over one field, then $(2)$ holds; applying $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$ over any other field proves the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{finite-orbit-isotropy}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a countable discrete groupoid, let $O\subseteq\mathcal G^{(0)}$ be a finite orbit, and let $u\in O$. Then the reduction $\mathcal G|_O$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$ if and only if the isotropy group $\mathcal G_u^u$ is amenable.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The reduction $\mathcal G|_O$ is a transitive discrete groupoid with finite unit space $O$, and its isotropy group at $u$ is $\mathcal G_u^u$. The conclusion follows from Theorem~\ref{finite-transitive-isotropy}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{finite-versus-infinite-orbits}
Lemma~\ref{infinite-transitive-discrete-groupoid} and Theorem~\ref{finite-transitive-isotropy} exhibit a sharp dichotomy. On an infinite orbit, source anchoring still permits the F{\o}lner subspace to escape through a range unit not seen by the prescribed finite-dimensional multiplier space, so the isotropy may be non-amenable. On a finite orbit, no such escape is possible: the finite matrix amplification forces the F{\o}lner estimate to descend to the isotropy group algebra.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{hereditarily-algebraically-amenable}
A Hausdorff ample groupoid $\mathcal G$ is called \emph{hereditarily source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$} if every non-empty Hausdorff ample subgroupoid $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$, endowed with the subspace topology, is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{hereditary-discrete-characterization}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a countable discrete groupoid. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathcal G$ is hereditarily source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$;
    \item every isotropy group $\mathcal G_u^u$, with $u\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$, is amenable.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if these conditions hold for one field, then they hold for every field.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Assume first that $\mathcal G$ is hereditarily source-anchored left algebraically amenable. Fix $u\in\mathcal G^{(0)}$. The isotropy group $\mathcal G_u^u$, viewed as a one-unit groupoid, is a discrete Hausdorff ample subgroupoid of $\mathcal G$. Hence it is source-anchored left algebraically amenable. By Theorem~\ref{group-case}, the group $\mathcal G_u^u$ is amenable. This proves $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$.

Conversely, suppose that every isotropy group of $\mathcal G$ is amenable. Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$ be a non-empty subgroupoid. Since $\mathcal G$ is discrete, $\mathcal H$ is also a countable discrete Hausdorff ample groupoid. For every $u\in\mathcal H^{(0)}$,
$$
\mathcal H_u^u\leq\mathcal G_u^u.
$$
Subgroups of amenable groups are amenable, so every isotropy group of $\mathcal H$ is amenable.

Decompose $\mathcal H$ into its orbit subgroupoids:
$$
\mathcal H=\bigsqcup_{O\in\mathcal H^{(0)}/\mathcal H}\mathcal H|_O.
$$
Because $\mathcal H$ is discrete, each orbit subgroupoid is open, and the displayed decomposition is a topological disjoint union. Each $\mathcal H|_O$ is transitive. If $O$ is infinite, Lemma~\ref{infinite-transitive-discrete-groupoid} shows that $\mathcal H|_O$ is algebraically amenable. If $O$ is finite, its isotropy groups are amenable, and Theorem~\ref{finite-transitive-isotropy} gives the same conclusion. Proposition~\ref{disjoint-unions} now implies that $\mathcal H$ is algebraically amenable. Since $\mathcal H$ was arbitrary, $\mathcal G$ is hereditarily source-anchored left algebraically amenable. This proves $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$.

Condition $(2)$ is independent of the coefficient field. Hence the equivalence shows that the hereditary property is also independent of the field in the countable discrete setting.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{hereditary-discrete-classes}
Each of the following countable discrete groupoids is hereditarily source-anchored left algebraically amenable over every field:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item every principal groupoid;
    \item every groupoid whose isotropy groups are finite;
    \item every groupoid whose isotropy groups are abelian, locally finite or solvable;
    \item every topological disjoint union of amenable groups.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
A principal groupoid has trivial isotropy groups. Finite, abelian, locally finite and solvable groups are amenable, as recalled in Section~\ref{preliminaries}. A disjoint union of amenable groups has amenable isotropy at every unit. Theorem~\ref{hereditary-discrete-characterization} applies in each case.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{subgroupoid-summary}
The subgroupoid picture can now be summarized as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Open invariant reductions, equivalently open source-saturated subgroupoids, inherit algebraic amenability from the ambient groupoid by Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction}.
    \item Arbitrary open subgroupoids need not inherit the property, by Proposition~\ref{arbitrary-subgroupoids-fail}.
    \item Requiring hereditary algebraic amenability restores the subgroup property by definition, and Theorem~\ref{hereditary-discrete-characterization} gives an exact criterion in the countable discrete case: all isotropy groups must be amenable.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the classical subgroup property is recovered in the one-unit case and in the hereditary discrete class described above. These are positive cases, not an exhaustive classification of subgroupoid inclusions for which inheritance holds.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
\label{transformation-groupoid-definition}
The \emph{transformation groupoid} $X\rtimes G$ is the set $X\times G$ with range and source maps
$$
r(x,g)=x,\ s(x,g)=g^{-1}x,
$$
composition $(x,g)(g^{-1}x,h)=(x,gh)$, and inversion
$$
(x,g)^{-1}=(g^{-1}x,g^{-1}).
$$
Its unit space is identified with $X$ through $x\mapsto(x,e_G)$, and its topology is the product topology. We use the range-first convention for its arrows.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{transformation-homogeneous-model}
The groupoid $X\rtimes G$ is Hausdorff and ample. Its rectangular compact open bisections satisfy
$$
(D_1\times\{g\})(D_2\times\{h\})=(D_1\cap gD_2)\times\{gh\}
$$
for clopen $D_1,D_2\subseteq X$. Every compact open bisection $U$ has a finite disjoint decomposition
$$
U=\bigsqcup_{g\in K_U}D_{U,g}\times\{g\},
$$
where $K_U\subseteq G$ is finite and each $D_{U,g}$ is clopen.

For $g\in G$, set $u_g=\mathbf 1_{X\times\{g\}}$. Then $u_g$ is invertible in $A_G$, with inverse $u_{g^{-1}}$, and
$$
u_g u_h=u_{gh},\ u_g f=(f\circ g^{-1})u_g\quad(f\in D).
$$
Every element of $A_G$ has a unique finite expression $\sum_g f_g u_g$, with $f_g\in D$, and also a unique finite expression $\sum_g u_g d_g$, with $d_g\in D$. In particular,
$$
A_G=\bigoplus_{g\in G}D u_g
=\bigoplus_{g\in G}u_g D.
$$
All products in these formulas are convolution products.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
On $D_1\times\{g\}$, the range and source maps are homeomorphisms onto $D_1$ and $g^{-1}D_1$, respectively. Such sets form a compact open basis, and $X\times G$ is Hausdorff. The multiplication formula follows by checking composability. The projection of a compact open bisection $U$ onto the discrete space $G$ is finite; its slices $D_{U,g}$ are open and compact in $X$, hence clopen. This proves the decomposition.
