The convolution identities follow from the rectangular multiplication formula. In particular, $u_{e_G}=\mathbf 1_X$ is the identity and $u_g u_{g^{-1}}=u_{g^{-1}}u_g=\mathbf 1_X$. If $a\in A_G$, compactness of its support implies that only finitely many slices $X\times\{g\}$ meet that support. Its restriction to each such slice is a function $f_g\in D$, giving $a=\sum_g f_g u_g$. The expression is unique because distinct slices are disjoint. Since
$$
f_g u_g=u_g(f_g\circ g),
$$
the right-coefficient expression is also unique.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{amenable-compact-transformation}
If $G$ is amenable, then $X\rtimes G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over every field.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Fix a non-empty clopen set $C\subseteq X$, a finite-dimensional space $L\subseteq A_G$, and $\varepsilon>0$. We use Proposition~\ref{anchored-finite-dimensional-test}. If $L=\{0\}$, the space $\Bbbk\mathbf 1_C$ suffices. Otherwise, choose a basis $a_1,\dots,a_q$ of $L$ and a finite set $K\subseteq G$ containing $e_G$ such that
$$
a_i=\sum_{k\in K}f_{i,k}u_k,\ f_{i,k}\in D.
$$

The group F{\o}lner condition gives a non-empty finite set $F\subseteq G$ with
$$
|KF|\leq(1+\varepsilon)|F|.
$$
Indeed, choose $F$ so that $|kF\setminus F|<\varepsilon|F|/|K|$ for every $k\in K$. Since $e_G\in K$, the union bound gives the displayed estimate. This version follows from the condition in the preliminaries by applying it to $K^{-1}$ and using $|kF\setminus F|=|F\setminus k^{-1}F|$.

The finitely many functions
$$
(f_{i,k}\circ h)|_C,\ 1\leq i\leq q,\ k\in K,\ h\in KF,
$$
are locally constant on the compact space $C$. Each has finite image, and their fibers are clopen. The non-empty intersections of these fibers therefore form a finite clopen partition $\mathcal{Q}$ of $C$ on whose members all these functions are constant. Its members are also clopen in $X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq G$, put
$$
W(S,\mathcal{Q})=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{u_s\mathbf 1_P\mid s\in S,\ P\in\mathcal{Q}\}.
$$
Since $u_s\mathbf 1_P=\mathbf 1_{sP\times\{s\}}$, these functions have pairwise disjoint non-empty supports. Consequently,
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}W(S,\mathcal{Q})=|S|\,|\mathcal{Q}|.
$$
Moreover, their sources lie in $P\subseteq C$, so $W(S,\mathcal{Q})\subseteq A_G\mathbf 1_C$.

Take $W=W(F,\mathcal{Q})$. For $f\in F$ and $P\in\mathcal{Q}$, we have
$$
a_i(u_f\mathbf 1_P)=\sum_{k\in K}f_{i,k}u_{kf}\mathbf 1_P.
$$
The function $f_{i,k}$ is constant on $kfP$, by the choice of $\mathcal{Q}$. Writing this constant as $\lambda_{i,k,f,P}$, we obtain
$$
f_{i,k}u_{kf}\mathbf 1_P=\lambda_{i,k,f,P}u_{kf}\mathbf 1_P.
$$
Thus $LW\subseteq W(KF,\mathcal{Q})$. Since $F\subseteq KF$, also $W\subseteq W(KF,\mathcal{Q})$, and hence
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq |KF|\,|\mathcal{Q}|\leq(1+\varepsilon)|F|\,|\mathcal{Q}|=(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
The space $W$ is non-zero and has the prescribed source anchor.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{finite-regular-copies-folner}
Let $R$ be a non-zero unital $\Bbbk$-algebra, let $E\subseteq R$ be finite-dimensional with $1_R\in E$, let $m\geq1$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $R$ act coordinatewise on $R^m$. If a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq R^m$ satisfies
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(EW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W),
$$
then there is a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $V\subseteq R$ such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Put $U=EW$, and let
$$
F_j=R^j\oplus\{0\}^{m-j}\subseteq R^m, \ 0\leq j\leq m.
$$
For $1\leq j\leq m$, let $\pi_j$ be the $j$th coordinate projection and define
$$
V_j=\pi_j(W\cap F_j),\ Z_j=\pi_j(U\cap F_j).
$$
The kernel of $\pi_j$ on $W\cap F_j$ is $W\cap F_{j-1}$. The corresponding assertion holds for $U$. Rank-nullity and telescoping therefore give
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=\sum_{j=1}^m\dim_{\Bbbk}(V_j),\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(U)=\sum_{j=1}^m\dim_{\Bbbk}(Z_j).
$$

For $a\in E$ and $w\in W\cap F_j$, the vector $aw$ belongs to $U\cap F_j$ and has $j$th coordinate $a\pi_j(w)$. It follows that $EV_j\subseteq Z_j$. Thus
$$
\sum_{j=1}^m\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV_j)\leq\dim_{\Bbbk}(U)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\sum_{j=1}^m\dim_{\Bbbk}(V_j).
$$
At least one $V_j$ is non-zero because $W\neq\{0\}$. If every non-zero $V_j$ violated the desired inequality, summing those strict violations would contradict the last display. Choosing an index for which it holds and setting $V=V_j$ proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{compact-transformation-criterion}
Under the standing hypotheses on $G\curvearrowright X$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is amenable;
\item $A_{\Bbbk}(X\rtimes G)$ is left algebraically amenable;
\item $X\rtimes G$ is weakly left bisectionally algebraically amenable;
\item $X\rtimes G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, these properties are independent of the coefficient field for global actions on non-empty compact zero-dimensional spaces.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{amenable-compact-transformation} gives $(1)\Rightarrow(4)$, Proposition~\ref{anchored-implies-weak} gives $(4)\Rightarrow(3)$, and Proposition~\ref{weak-bisectional-equivalence} gives $(3)\Leftrightarrow(2)$.

Assume $(2)$ and identify $R=\Bbbk G$ with the unital subalgebra spanned by the $u_g$. Let $E\subseteq R$ be any finite-dimensional subspace containing $1_R$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Algebraic amenability of $A_G$ provides a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A_G$ such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(EW)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+EW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$

Expand a basis of $W$ in the right-coefficient form $\sum_g u_g d_g$ from Lemma~\ref{transformation-homogeneous-model}. There are only finitely many coefficient functions in these expansions. Choose a finite clopen partition $\mathcal{Q}$ of $X$ on whose members every one of these functions is constant. Then
$$
W\subseteq M_{\mathcal{Q}}:=\bigoplus_{P\in\mathcal{Q}}R\mathbf 1_P.
$$
This is a free left $R$-module of rank $|\mathcal{Q}|$. To verify freeness, expand a finite relation $\sum_P r_P\mathbf 1_P=0$ using $r_P=\sum_g\lambda_{g,P}u_g$. The functions $u_g\mathbf 1_P=\mathbf 1_{gP\times\{g\}}$ have pairwise disjoint non-empty supports as $(g,P)$ varies, so every $\lambda_{g,P}$ is zero. Furthermore,
$$
u_h(u_g\mathbf 1_P)=u_{hg}\mathbf 1_P,
$$
so the identification $M_{\mathcal{Q}}\cong R^{|\mathcal{Q}|}$ intertwines left multiplication by $R$ with coordinatewise multiplication. In particular, $EW\subseteq M_{\mathcal{Q}}$.

Lemma~\ref{finite-regular-copies-folner} now gives a non-zero finite-dimensional $V\subseteq R$ with
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(V+EV)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(EV)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(V).
$$
Testing subspaces $E$ containing $1_R$ suffices, since any finite-dimensional subspace can be enlarged by $\Bbbk1_R$. Hence $R=\Bbbk G$ is left algebraically amenable. Bartholdi's criterion, recalled in Theorem~\ref{bartholdi-group-algebra}, implies that $G$ is amenable; see \cite[Corollary 1.5]{Bartholdi08}. This proves $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$.

The equivalence with group amenability holds for every field, which proves the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{compact-action-scope}
The theorem concerns the algebraic F{\o}lner conditions defined here, not topological amenability of a group action. Within this compact global-action setting, the weak and source-anchored properties coincide and depend only on the acting group. This does not assert the same equivalence for arbitrary ample groupoids, partial actions or groupoids of germs.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{finite-index-coset-model}
There is a direct-sum decomposition of right $B$-modules
$$
A=\bigoplus_{t\in T}u_tB.
$$
For each $g\in G$ and $t\in T$, let $\sigma_g(t)\in T$ and $h(g,t)\in H$ be determined by
$$
gt=\sigma_g(t)h(g,t).
$$
Then $\sigma_g$ permutes $T$. If $D_0\subseteq X$ is clopen, then
$$
\mathbf 1_{D_0\times\{g\}}u_t=u_{\sigma_g(t)}\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\sigma_g(t)^{-1}D_0}u_{h(g,t)}\bigr),
$$
where the expression in parentheses belongs to $B$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Every term $u_gd$, with $d\in D$, can be written uniquely as $u_t(u_hd)$ once $g=th$ is its coset decomposition. Hence the displayed spaces span $A$. The support of $u_tB$ has labels in $tH$, so different summands have disjoint sets of labels and their sum is direct. Left multiplication by $u_t$ is a linear isomorphism from $B$ onto $u_tB$, with inverse left multiplication by $u_{t^{-1}}$.

Left multiplication by $g$ is a bijection of the finite coset space $G/H$, giving the permutation $\sigma_g$. Finally, Lemma~\ref{transformation-homogeneous-model} yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
u_{\sigma_g(t)}\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\sigma_g(t)^{-1}D_0}u_{h(g,t)}\bigr) &=\mathbf 1_{D_0}u_{\sigma_g(t)h(g,t)}\\
&=\mathbf 1_{D_0}u_{gt}=\mathbf 1_{D_0\times\{g\}}u_t.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $h(g,t)\in H$, the coefficient belongs to $B$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{finite-index-folner-induction}
Let $L\subseteq A$ be finite-dimensional. There is a finite-dimensional subspace $E\subseteq B$, containing $1_B$, with the following property. For every non-empty clopen $C\subseteq X$ and every non-zero finite-dimensional $W_0\subseteq B\mathbf 1_C$, the space
$$
W=\bigoplus_{t\in T}u_tW_0
$$
satisfies
$$
W\subseteq A\mathbf 1_C,\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=n\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0),
$$
and
$$
\frac{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)-\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)}{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)}\leq\frac{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0+EW_0)-\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0)}{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0)}.
$$
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Choose a basis $a_1,\dots,a_q$ of $L$. For each $i$ and $t\in T$, use Lemma~\ref{finite-index-coset-model} to write
$$
a_i u_t=\sum_{s\in T}u_s b_{i,s,t},\ b_{i,s,t}\in B.
$$
Set
$$
E=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\bigl(\{1_B\}\cup\{b_{i,s,t}\mid 1\leq i\leq q,\ s,t\in T\}\bigr).
$$
This space is finite-dimensional, depends only on $L$ and the chosen transversal, and works also for $L=\{0\}$ by taking $E=\Bbbk1_B$.

For $w\in W_0$, we have $w\mathbf 1_C=w$, so
$$
(u_tw)\mathbf 1_C=u_t(w\mathbf 1_C)=u_tw.
$$
Thus every $u_tW_0$ lies in $A\mathbf 1_C$. Their sum is direct by the coset support decomposition, and each has dimension $\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0)$ because $u_t$ is invertible. This proves the containment and dimension assertion.

Let $Q=W_0+EW_0$. Since $B\mathbf 1_C$ is a left ideal of $B$, we have $Q\subseteq B\mathbf 1_C$. For each $i,t$, and $w\in W_0$,
$$
a_i(u_tw)=\sum_{s\in T}u_s b_{i,s,t}w\in\bigoplus_{s\in T}u_sQ.
$$
The same direct sum contains $W$, because $W_0\subseteq Q$. Consequently,
$$
W+LW\subseteq\bigoplus_{s\in T}u_sQ,\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq n\dim_{\Bbbk}(Q).
$$
Subtract $\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=n\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0)$ and divide by this positive number. The required relative-boundary estimate follows.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{finite-index-transformation}
Let $H\leq G$ have finite index. If $X\rtimes H$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$, then $X\rtimes G$ is source-anchored left algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Let $C\subseteq X$ be non-empty and clopen, let $L\subseteq A_G$ be finite-dimensional, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $E\subseteq A_H$ from Proposition~\ref{finite-index-folner-induction}. By the hypothesis and Proposition~\ref{anchored-finite-dimensional-test}, there exists a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W_0\subseteq A_H\mathbf 1_C$ such that
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0+EW_0)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0).
$$
Set $W=\bigoplus_{t\in T}u_tW_0$. Quantitative induction gives $W\subseteq A_G\mathbf 1_C$, $W\neq\{0\}$, and
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
Proposition~\ref{anchored-finite-dimensional-test} now proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
The induction argument keeps the same source anchor $C$. It uses neither normality of $H$ nor division by $[G:H]$ inside $\Bbbk$, and therefore applies in every characteristic. Its conclusion could also be deduced from Theorem~\ref{compact-transformation-criterion} and the classical finite-index permanence property for groups. The direct proof supplies additional quantitative information: the dimension is multiplied by $[G:H]$, but the relative boundary does not increase.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{compact-action-subgroup-restriction}
Let $H\leq G$ be any subgroup. If $X\rtimes G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$, then $X\rtimes H$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$. If $[G:H]<\infty$, then
$$
X\rtimes H\text{ is algebraically amenable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\rtimes G\text{ is algebraically amenable}.
$$
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{compact-transformation-criterion}, amenability of $X\rtimes G$ implies amenability of $G$. Its subgroup $H$ is amenable by the classical subgroup property recalled in Section~\ref{preliminaries}. Proposition~\ref{amenable-compact-transformation}, applied to the restricted action, gives amenability of $X\rtimes H$. When the index is finite, the converse is Theorem~\ref{finite-index-transformation}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{compact-action-finite-orbit}
Suppose that $O\subseteq X$ is a finite clopen $G$-orbit and let $x\in O$. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X\rtimes G$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$;
\item $(X\rtimes G)|_O$ is algebraically amenable over $\Bbbk$;
\item the stabilizer $G_x=\{g\in G\mid gx=x\}$ is amenable;
\item $G$ is amenable.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The reduction is $O\rtimes G$. It is a countable transitive discrete groupoid because $O$ is a finite Hausdorff space. Its isotropy at $x$ consists of $(x,g)$ with $g\in G_x$, and is isomorphic to $G_x$. Thus Theorem~\ref{finite-transitive-isotropy} gives $(2)\Leftrightarrow(3)$. Applying Theorem~\ref{compact-transformation-criterion} first to $X$ and then to the non-empty compact space $O$ gives $(1)\Leftrightarrow(4)\Leftrightarrow(2)$. The clopen hypothesis also makes the passage from $(1)$ to $(2)$ an instance of Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{dihedral-compact-action}
Let $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$, and define homeomorphisms $T,J:X\to X$ by
$$
(Tx)_j=x_{j+1},\qquad (Jx)_j=x_{-j}.
$$
They satisfy $J^2=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $JTJ=T^{-1}$. Hence $r\mapsto T$ and $s\mapsto J$ define an action of the infinite dihedral group
$$
D_{\infty}=\langle r,s\mid s^2=e,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle.
$$
The subgroup $H=\langle r\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$ has index two and transversal $\{e,s\}$. Proposition~\ref{amenable-compact-transformation} makes $X\rtimes H$ algebraically amenable, and Theorem~\ref{finite-index-transformation} gives the same conclusion for $X\rtimes D_{\infty}$.

More explicitly, for a prescribed anchor $C$, multiplier space $L$ and error $\varepsilon$, form the coefficient space $E$ from Proposition~\ref{finite-index-folner-induction}. Choose an anchored $(E,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace $W_0$ for $A_H$ by the clopen-partition construction above. Then
$$
W=W_0\oplus u_sW_0,\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=2\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_0),
$$
is an anchored $(L,\varepsilon)$-F{\o}lner subspace for $A_{\Bbbk}(X\rtimes D_{\infty})$. This gives a concrete noncommutative example on a nondiscrete compact unit space, with no restriction on the characteristic of $\Bbbk$.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
Let $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$, let $G=F_2$ act trivially on $X$, and take $H=\{e_G\}$. Then $X\rtimes H$ is the unit groupoid on $X$ and is algebraically amenable. However, $X\rtimes G$ is not algebraically amenable by Theorem~\ref{compact-transformation-criterion}, since $F_2$ is not amenable. Here $[G:H]=\infty$, so this does not contradict the induction theorem. Thus amenability of a restricted action alone cannot justify ascent to an arbitrary larger acting group.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{noncompact-regular-action}
Let $G=F_2$ and let $X=G$ with the discrete topology and the left translation action. This space is locally compact and zero-dimensional, but not compact. The map
$$
X\rtimes G\longrightarrow G\times G,\ (x,g)\longmapsto(x,g^{-1}x),
$$
is an isomorphism onto the pair groupoid, with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy^{-1})$. It intertwines range, source and composition, and both topologies are discrete. The pair groupoid is transitive with infinite unit space, so Lemma~\ref{infinite-transitive-discrete-groupoid} shows that $X\rtimes G$ is source-anchored algebraically amenable even though $G$ is not amenable.

In this example, $X\times\{g\}$ is not compact, so its characteristic function is not an element of the Steinberg algebra. The global units $u_g$ used in the compact-action criterion are therefore absent. This explains why that argument does not rule out range escape for noncompact actions.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{ex:unit-groupoids}
Let $X$ be a non-empty locally compact Hausdorff space with a basis of compact open subsets. Regard $X$ as a groupoid $\mathcal U_X$ containing only unit arrows. Thus $r(x)=s(x)=x$, and the only composable pairs are $(x,x)$, with product $xx=x$. Its Steinberg algebra is
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal U_X)=C_c^{\mathrm{lc}}(X,\Bbbk),
$$
where $C_c^{\mathrm{lc}}(X,\Bbbk)$ denotes the algebra of locally constant, compactly supported functions, with pointwise multiplication. This follows directly from the convolution construction recalled in Section~\ref{preliminaries}; see also \cite[\S 3]{Ste09}.

Fix a non-empty compact open subset $C\subseteq X$ and a finite-dimensional subspace $L$ of this algebra. Choose a basis $f_1,\dots,f_q$ of $L$ and a point $x_0\in C$. Local constancy and the compact open basis give a non-empty compact open neighborhood $D$ of $x_0$, contained in $C$, on which every $f_i$ is constant. When $L=\{0\}$, no local constancy conditions are needed, and one may take $D=C$.

Set
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_D\}.
$$
Then $W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal U_X)\mathbf 1_C$ and $\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=1$. For every $i$,
$$
f_i\mathbf 1_D=f_i(x_0)\mathbf 1_D,
$$
so $LW\subseteq W$. Hence $W+LW=W$, and the algebraic boundary is zero. Therefore $\mathcal U_X$ is algebraically amenable over every field.

For instance, taking $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ gives a nondiscrete example with an infinite-dimensional algebra: the characteristic functions of the binary cylinders of any fixed length are linearly independent, and the number of such cylinders is unbounded. Moreover, every Hausdorff ample subgroupoid of $\mathcal U_X$ is itself a unit groupoid, so the same argument proves hereditary algebraic amenability in this family.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
\label{ex:abelian-group-bundles}
Let $X$ be as in Example~\ref{ex:unit-groupoids}, and let $d\geq 1$. Define
$$
\mathcal B_d=X\times\mathbb Z^d,\ r(x,g)=s(x,g)=x,
$$
with multiplication $(x,g)(x,h)=(x,g+h)$ and inversion $(x,g)^{-1}=(x,-g)$. Equip $\mathcal B_d$ with the product topology, using the discrete topology on $\mathbb Z^d$. The sets $D\times\{g\}$, with $D\subseteq X$ compact open, form a basis of compact open bisections. Thus $\mathcal B_d$ is Hausdorff and ample. All its orbits are singletons, while its isotropy group at every unit is $\mathbb Z^d$.

For $f\in C_c^{\mathrm{lc}}(X,\Bbbk)$ and $g\in\mathbb Z^d$, write $f\delta_g$ for the function defined by
$$
(f\delta_g)(x,h)=f(x)\mathbf 1_{\{g\}}(h).
$$
Compact support implies that every element of $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal B_d)$ is a finite sum of such functions. Convolution gives
$$
(f\delta_g)\ast(h\delta_t)=(fh)\delta_{g+t}.
$$
Consequently,
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal B_d)\cong C_c^{\mathrm{lc}}(X,\Bbbk)\otimes_{\Bbbk}\Bbbk\mathbb Z^d.
$$

We give a direct source-anchored F{\o}lner construction. Fix a non-empty compact open subset $C\subseteq X$, a finite-dimensional subspace $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal B_d)$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a basis $a_1,\dots,a_q$ of $L$ and a finite set $T\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ such that
$$
a_i=\sum_{g\in T}f_{i,g}\delta_g,\ f_{i,g}\in C_c^{\mathrm{lc}}(X,\Bbbk).
$$
Choose $x_0\in C$ and a non-empty compact open neighborhood $D\subseteq C$ of $x_0$ on which every coefficient function $f_{i,g}$ is constant. The case $L=\{0\}$ is included by taking $T=\varnothing$ and $D=C$.

Choose an integer $m\geq 0$ such that $T\cup\{0\}\subseteq[-m,m]^d$, and for every integer $N\geq 1$ put
$$
F_N=[-N,N]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d,\ W_N=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_D\delta_f\mid f\in F_N\}.
$$
The basis functions have disjoint supports, so
$$
W_N\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal B_d)\mathbf 1_C,\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(W_N)=(2N+1)^d.
$$
For each $i$ and $f\in F_N$,
$$
a_i\ast(\mathbf 1_D\delta_f)=\sum_{g\in T}f_{i,g}(x_0)\mathbf 1_D\delta_{g+f}.
$$
Since $g+f\in F_{N+m}$, this implies $W_N+LW_N\subseteq W_{N+m}$. Therefore
$$
\frac{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_N+LW_N)}{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_N)}\leq\left(\frac{2N+2m+1}{2N+1}\right)^d\longrightarrow 1.
$$
For sufficiently large $N$, the required F{\o}lner inequality follows. Thus $\mathcal B_d$ is algebraically amenable over every field.

When $X$ is a point, the algebra is the Laurent polynomial algebra $\Bbbk[t_1^{\pm1},\dots,t_d^{\pm1}]$. For a Cantor space $X$, the same construction gives nondiscrete examples with nontrivial infinite isotropy. In this case the approximation takes place in the isotropy directions, rather than by escaping to new range units.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
\label{ex:finite-matrix-groupoids}
Let $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$, where $n\geq 1$, and let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group. The discrete transitive groupoid
$$
\mathcal M_n(\Gamma)=I_n\times\Gamma\times I_n
$$
has range $r(i,g,j)=i$, source $s(i,g,j)=j$, multiplication
$$
(i,g,j)(j,h,k)=(i,gh,k),
$$
and inversion $(i,g,j)^{-1}=(j,g^{-1},i)$. Its matrix model is
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal M_n(\Gamma))\cong M_n(\Bbbk\Gamma),\ \mathbf 1_{\{(i,g,j)\}}\longmapsto E_{ij}(g),
$$
where $E_{ij}(a)$ denotes the matrix with entry $a$ in position $(i,j)$ and zero elsewhere. This is the model of Lemma~\ref{finite-transitive-matrix-model}; see also \cite[Example 3.2 and Proposition 4.3]{ClarkHazrat20}.

For $\Gamma=\mathbb Z$, identify $\Bbbk\Gamma$ with $\Bbbk[t,t^{-1}]$. Let $C\subseteq I_n$ be non-empty, choose $j\in C$, and write
$$
e_C=\sum_{c\in C}E_{cc}(1).
$$
Given a finite-dimensional subspace $L\subseteq M_n(\Bbbk[t,t^{-1}])$, choose $m\geq 0$ such that every entry of every matrix in $L$ is a linear combination of $t^p$ with $|p|\leq m$. For $N\geq 1$, set
$$
W_N=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{E_{ij}(t^q)\mid 1\leq i\leq n,\ -N\leq q\leq N\}.
$$
Then $W_N\subseteq M_n(\Bbbk[t,t^{-1}])e_C$ and
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_N)=n(2N+1).
$$
The identity
$$
E_{ab}(t^p)E_{ij}(t^q)=\delta_{b,i}E_{aj}(t^{p+q})
$$
shows that $W_N+LW_N\subseteq W_{N+m}$. Hence
$$
\frac{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_N+LW_N)}{\dim_{\Bbbk}(W_N)}\leq\frac{2N+2m+1}{2N+1}=1+\frac{2m}{2N+1}.
$$
Thus finite matrix amplification preserves these explicit F{\o}lner approximations.

More generally, Theorem~\ref{finite-transitive-isotropy} gives
$$
\mathcal M_n(\Gamma)\text{ is algebraically amenable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Gamma\text{ is amenable}.
$$
In particular, $\mathcal M_n(\mathbb Z^d)$ is algebraically amenable, whereas $\mathcal M_n(F_2)$ is not, since $F_2$ is non-amenable; see \cite[Theorem 5]{Cortez22}. Thus neither a finite unit space nor finite matrix amplification removes the obstruction carried by non-amenable isotropy.
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
\label{ex:binary-tail-equivalence}
Let $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ with the product topology, and let $\sigma:X\to X$ be the left shift. Consider the tail-equivalence groupoid
$$
\mathcal R=\{(x,y)\in X\times X\mid\sigma^n(x)=\sigma^n(y)\text{ for some }n\geq 0\},
$$
with $r(x,y)=x$, $s(x,y)=y$, inversion $(x,y)^{-1}=(y,x)$, and multiplication $(x,y)(y,z)=(x,z)$.

If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are binary words of the same finite length, define
$$
Z(\alpha,\beta)=\{(\alpha z,\beta z)\mid z\in X\}.
$$
Here $\alpha z$ denotes concatenation. Equip $\mathcal R$ with the topology having these sets as a basis, rather than the subspace topology inherited from $X\times X$. Each $Z(\alpha,\beta)$ is a compact open bisection, with range $\alpha X$ and source $\beta X$. These charts make $\mathcal R$ a Hausdorff ample groupoid with unit space $X$.

For $n\geq 0$, put
$$
\mathcal R_n=\{(x,y)\in X\times X\mid\sigma^n(x)=\sigma^n(y)\}.
$$
It is the finite disjoint union of the bisections $Z(\alpha,\beta)$ with $|\alpha|=|\beta|=n$. Hence $\mathcal R_n$ is compact, open and principal, and $\mathcal R_n^{(0)}=X$. Moreover,
$$
\mathcal R_n\subseteq\mathcal R_{n+1},\ \mathcal R=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\mathcal R_n.
$$
Thus $\mathcal R$ is an AF groupoid in the sense of Definition~\ref{af-groupoid-definition}; compare \cite[\S 5.2]{ClarkHazrat20}.

To exhibit the F{\o}lner subspaces explicitly, set
$$
b_{\alpha,\beta}=\mathbf 1_{Z(\alpha,\beta)}, \ B_n=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}
\{b_{\alpha,\beta}\mid |\alpha|=|\beta|=n\}.
$$
For words of length $n$, convolution gives
$$
b_{\alpha,\beta}\ast b_{\gamma,\delta}=\delta_{\beta,\gamma}b_{\alpha,\delta}.
$$
The supports are pairwise disjoint, so these functions are linearly independent matrix units. Consequently,
$$
B_n\cong M_{2^n}(\Bbbk),\ \sum_{|\alpha|=n}b_{\alpha,\alpha}=\mathbf 1_X.
$$
The disjoint decomposition
$$
Z(\alpha,\beta)=Z(\alpha0,\beta0)\sqcup Z(\alpha1,\beta1)
$$
yields
$$
b_{\alpha,\beta}=b_{\alpha0,\beta0}+b_{\alpha1,\beta1},
$$
so $B_n\subseteq B_{n+1}$. Every locally constant, compactly supported function is a finite linear combination of characteristic functions of these basic bisections: cover its compact support by finitely many such bisections on which it is constant, and refine them to a common word length. Therefore
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal R)=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}B_n.
$$
The finite-dimensional algebras $B_n$ should not be confused with the full algebras $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal R_n)$, which allow arbitrary locally constant dependence on the common infinite tail.

Now let $C\subseteq X$ be non-empty compact open and let $L\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal R)$ be finite-dimensional. Choose $n$ large enough that $L\subseteq B_n$ and $C$ is a union of cylinders of length $n$. If $\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$ is the non-empty collection of words defining those cylinders, then
$$
\mathbf 1_C=\sum_{\beta\in\mathcal C}b_{\beta,\beta}\in B_n.
$$
Set $W=B_n\mathbf 1_C$. The matrix units give
$$
W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{b_{\alpha,\beta}\mid |\alpha|=n,\ \beta\in\mathcal C\},\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=2^n|\mathcal C|.
$$
In particular, $W\neq\{0\}$ and $W\subseteq A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal R)\mathbf 1_C$. Since $L\subseteq B_n$,
$$
LW\subseteq B_n(B_n\mathbf 1_C)\subseteq B_n\mathbf 1_C=W.
$$
Thus the algebraic boundary is zero. This realizes Corollary~\ref{af-groupoids} concretely in an infinite-dimensional, noncommutative Steinberg algebra with nondiscrete unit space.
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\label{ex:infinite-matrix-amplification}
Let $\Gamma=F_2$, and equip
$$
\mathcal M_{\infty}(\Gamma)=\mathbb N\times\Gamma\times\mathbb N
$$
with the discrete topology and the same operations as in Example~\ref{ex:finite-matrix-groupoids}. Its Steinberg algebra identifies with
$$
M_{\mathbb N}^{\mathrm{fin}}(\Bbbk\Gamma),
$$
the algebra of matrices over $\Bbbk\Gamma$ with only finitely many non-zero entries in total. Indeed, the assignment $\mathbf 1_{\{(i,g,j)\}}\mapsto E_{ij}(g)$ maps the natural basis to the matrix group-element basis and respects multiplication.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb N$ be non-empty and finite, and let $L$ be a finite-dimensional multiplier space. The union $S$ of the supports of a basis of $L$ is finite. Consequently,
$$
s(S)=\{s(\alpha)\mid\alpha\in S\}
$$
is finite. Choose $i_0\in\mathbb N\setminus s(S)$ and $c_0\in C$, and put
$$
\beta=(i_0,e_{\Gamma},c_0),\ W=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{\mathbf 1_{\{\beta\}}\}.
$$
Since $s(\beta)=c_0$, the space $W$ is contained in $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal M_{\infty}(\Gamma))\mathbf 1_C$. No $\alpha\in S$ can multiply $\beta$ on the left, because composability would require $s(\alpha)=i_0$. Hence
$$
LW=\{0\},\ \dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)=1.
$$
Thus $\mathcal M_{\infty}(F_2)$ is algebraically amenable over every field, as predicted by Lemma~\ref{infinite-transitive-discrete-groupoid}.

Nevertheless, for every $u\in\mathbb N$,
$$
\mathcal M_{\infty}(F_2)|_{\{u\}}=\{u\}\times F_2\times\{u\}\cong F_2
$$
is not algebraically amenable by Theorem~\ref{group-case}. In particular, the ambient groupoid is not hereditarily algebraically amenable. The set $\{u\}$ is compact open but not invariant, so this does not contradict Proposition~\ref{open-invariant-reduction}.

There is also a contrast with the directed-union result. Writing
$$
\mathcal M_{\infty}(F_2)=\bigcup_{n\geq 1}\mathcal M_n(F_2),
$$
we obtain an algebraically amenable directed union whose every displayed finite-unit stage is non-amenable. Thus the implication in Proposition~\ref{directed-unions} cannot be reversed. The zero boundary here is caused by range escape, not by amenability of the isotropy groups.
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
\label{ex:weak-versus-anchored}
Let $\mathcal T$ be the groupoid consisting of one unit and consider
$$
\mathcal D=\mathcal T\sqcup F_2.
$$
Then
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal D)\cong\Bbbk\oplus\Bbbk F_2.
$$
For every finite-dimensional subspace $L$ of this algebra, the fixed one-dimensional space
$$
W=\Bbbk\oplus\{0\}
$$
satisfies $LW\subseteq W$, because multiplication is componentwise. Therefore the algebra is algebraically amenable, and $\mathcal D$ is weakly bisectionally algebraically amenable by Proposition~\ref{weak-bisectional-equivalence}.

Let $u$ be the unit of the $F_2$ component. Anchoring at $C=\{u\}$ gives
$$
A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal D)\mathbf 1_C=\{0\}\oplus\Bbbk F_2.
$$
If $\mathcal D$ were source-anchored algebraically amenable, testing this anchor against every multiplier space of the form $\{0\}\oplus E$, with $E\subseteq\Bbbk F_2$ finite-dimensional, would make $\Bbbk F_2$ algebraically amenable. This contradicts Theorem~\ref{bartholdi-group-algebra}. Thus the weak and anchored properties differ even for a unital Steinberg algebra with a finite unit space.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
\label{ex:two-loop-obstruction}
Retain $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ and the shift $\sigma$ from Example~\ref{ex:binary-tail-equivalence}. Define
$$
\mathcal G_2=\{(x,m-n,y)\mid x,y\in X,\ m,n\geq 0,\ \sigma^m(x)=\sigma^n(y)\}.
$$
The range and source maps are $r(x,k,y)=x$ and $s(x,k,y)=y$, and the operations are
$$
(x,k,y)(y,\ell,z)=(x,k+\ell,z),\ (x,k,y)^{-1}=(y,-k,x).
$$
For arbitrary finite binary words $\alpha,\beta$, including the empty word, put
$$
Z_2(\alpha,\beta)=\{(\alpha z,|\alpha|-|\beta|,\beta z)\mid z\in X\}.
$$
These sets form the standard basis of compact open bisections. With this topology, $\mathcal G_2$ is the Hausdorff ample groupoid of the graph with one vertex and two loops; see \cite[\S 3.5]{ClarkHazrat20}.

Let $\varnothing$ denote the empty word, and, for $i\in\{0,1\}$, set
$$
U_i=Z_2(i,\varnothing),\ p_i=\mathbf 1_{U_i},\ q_i=\mathbf 1_{U_i^{-1}}.
$$
Each $U_i$ has source $X$ and range $iX$. The range sets $0X$ and $1X$ are disjoint and cover $X$. Bisection multiplication therefore gives
$$
q_i\ast p_j=\delta_{i,j}\mathbf 1_X,\ p_0\ast q_0+p_1\ast q_1=\mathbf 1_X.
$$
These are the familiar relations of the Leavitt algebra $L_{\Bbbk}(1,2)$, which identifies with $A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_2)$; see \cite[Example 4.4]{ClarkHazrat20} and \cite[Definition 5.1]{AraLiLledoWu18}.

The relations give a direct obstruction to algebraic F{\o}lner subspaces. Write $A=A_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal G_2)$ and take any non-zero finite-dimensional subspace $W\subseteq A$. The linear map
$$
W\oplus W\longrightarrow A,\ (w_0,w_1)\longmapsto p_0\ast w_0+p_1\ast w_1,
$$
is injective: multiplying a zero image on the left by $q_0$ gives $w_0=0$, and multiplying by $q_1$ gives $w_1=0$. Consequently,
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(p_0W+p_1W)=2\dim_{\Bbbk}(W).
$$
For the fixed two-dimensional multiplier space
$$
L=\operatorname{span}_{\Bbbk}\{p_0,p_1\},
$$
we therefore have
$$
\dim_{\Bbbk}(W+LW)\geq 2\dim_{\Bbbk}(W)
$$
for every non-zero finite-dimensional $W\subseteq A$. Taking $0<\varepsilon<1$ excludes the F{\o}lner inequality. Thus $A$ is not algebraically amenable, and $\mathcal G_2$ is neither weakly nor source-anchored algebraically amenable over any field. This calculation is the concrete two-loop instance of the obstruction discussed in \cite[Corollary 4.9]{AraLiLledoWu18}.

Nevertheless, every isotropy group of $\mathcal G_2$ is amenable. Indeed, for each $x\in X$, the map
$$
(\mathcal G_2)_x^x\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\ (x,k,x)\longmapsto k,
$$
is an injective group homomorphism. Hence the isotropy is trivial or infinite cyclic. Every orbit is also infinite: the distinct points $0^n1x$, for $n\geq 0$, all belong to the orbit of $x$, since $\sigma^{n+1}(0^n1x)=x$.

Thus amenable isotropy and infinite orbits do not imply source-anchored algebraic amenability in a nondiscrete groupoid. There is no contradiction with Theorem~\ref{hereditary-discrete-characterization} or Lemma~\ref{infinite-transitive-discrete-groupoid}, both of which require a discrete groupoid.

Finally, the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,0,y)$ identifies the AF groupoid $\mathcal R$ of Example~\ref{ex:binary-tail-equivalence} with the open subgroupoid of $\mathcal G_2$ consisting of degree-zero arrows. These two groupoids have the same unit space, but only $\mathcal R$ is algebraically amenable. In $\mathcal G_2$, the compact open bisections $U_0,U_1$ have full source $X$, but their ranges are the proper clopen subsets $0X$ and $1X$. Their left multipliers act on every source anchor, so moving the range cannot avoid the uniform dimension growth.
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
The examples separate the three approximation properties considered in the paper. Unit groupoids provide hereditary examples; infinite matrix amplification is source-anchored algebraically amenable but not hereditary; and $\mathcal T\sqcup F_2$ satisfies only the weak bisectional algebraic condition. The two-loop groupoid gives a further obstruction that is not detected by its individual isotropy groups. Thus the conditions depend not only on the groups attached to units, but also on how compact open bisections act across the unit space.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
